title: Kinetic Lifshitz invariants and dynamics of nonreciprocal fluctuations in superconductors
summary: We derive the generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory of a disordered noncentrosymmetric superconductor from the Keldysh nonlinear sigma model, using a two-dimensional electron gas with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and an in-plane Zeeman field as a minimal model. On the thermodynamic side we construct the Lifshitz invariants of the free energy, the linear and cubic gradient terms and the momentum-odd part of the quartic vertex, and trace their dependence on disorder. These couplings are governed by a single closed-form kernel controlled by the ratio of the Dyakonov-Perel spin-relaxation rate to temperature, interpolating between the weak-relaxation regime, where the invariants are suppressed, and the relaxation-dominated regime, where the helical modulation of the order parameter saturates at a universal, disorder-independent value. This crossover reconciles conflicting results for the magnetoelectric couplings of dirty Rashba superconductors. Because the theory is formulated on the Keldysh contour, it also determines the dissipative dynamics: the relaxation rate of a fluctuation with pair momentum $\mathbf{q}$, and hence, by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the Langevin noise power, acquires a term odd in $\mathbf{q}$ and odd in the magnetic field. The structure of this kinetic Lifshitz invariant is dictated by Onsager reciprocity: friction and noise renormalize in lockstep, so equal-time fluctuations remain Gibbsian while the dynamics are nonreciprocal. As applications we compute the superconducting diode efficiency near $T_c$, where the cubic invariant competes with the quartic vertex and with even higher-gradient terms rendered odd by the helical shift, reversing the sign of the diode coefficient, and the fluctuation-induced magnetochiral anisotropy above $T_c$, where the current-resolved nonreciprocal resistance forms a plateau across the Gaussian regime.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) theory for disordered noncentrosymmetric superconductors from the Keldysh nonlinear sigma model, using a 2D electron gas with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and an in-plane Zeeman field. It constructs thermodynamic Lifshitz invariants (linear/cubic gradient terms, momentum-odd quartic vertex) whose couplings are governed by a single closed-form kernel depending on the ratio of Dyakonov-Perel spin-relaxation rate to temperature. The theory also determines dissipative dynamics, including a q-odd, field-odd kinetic Lifshitz invariant constrained by Onsager reciprocity. Applications include computing the superconducting diode efficiency near Tc and fluctuation-induced magnetochiral anisotropy above Tc.
AI.motivation: To reconcile conflicting previous results for magnetoelectric couplings in dirty Rashba superconductors by deriving a unified microscopic TDGL theory that captures both thermodynamic and dissipative aspects within a single Keldysh framework.
AI.method: Starting from the Keldysh nonlinear sigma model, the authors derive the generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory for a disordered noncentrosymmetric superconductor. They obtain a single closed-form kernel controlling all Lifshitz-type couplings (linear and cubic gradient terms, momentum-odd quartic vertex) as a function of the ratio of Dyakonov-Perel spin-relaxation rate to temperature. The Keldysh formulation allows determination of dissipative dynamics: q-odd, field-odd relaxation rates and associated Langevin noise via the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Applications use this theory to compute superconducting diode efficiency near Tc and fluctuation-induced magnetochiral anisotropy above Tc.
AI.result: The couplings interpolate between a weak-relaxation regime where Lifshitz invariants are suppressed and a relaxation-dominated regime where helical modulation saturates at a universal, disorder-independent value. The kinetic Lifshitz invariant is dictated by Onsager reciprocity, ensuring friction and noise renormalize in lockstep. Near Tc, the cubic invariant competes with the quartic vertex and higher-gradient terms, reversing the sign of the diode coefficient. Above Tc, the current-resolved nonreciprocal resistance forms a plateau across the Gaussian regime.
AI.conclusion: The derived theory reconciles conflicting prior results for magnetoelectric couplings in dirty Rashba superconductors, provides a complete framework for nonreciprocal superconducting phenomena (diode effect and magnetochiral anisotropy) in both the thermodynamic and dissipative sectors, and demonstrates that Onsager reciprocity constrains the kinetic Lifshitz invariant to preserve Gibbsian equal-time fluctuations while allowing nonreciprocal dynamics.

title: Annular Majorana mode in a superconducting topological insulator
summary: When the surface states of a topological insulator becomes superconducting, topological superconductivity can be obtained, and each vortex on the surface can host one single Majorana zero-energy mode which is usually a wave packet decaying exponentially off the vortex core. Here, we predict stable Majorana zero-energy mode whose wave function is ring-shape, dubbed as annular Majorana mode, in the superconducting vortex in topological insulators respecting $3$-fold or $6$-fold rotational symmetry. Such topological insulators are featured with a single nonlinear Dirac cone located at $\barΓ$ or three linear Dirac cones at $\bar{\text{M}}$ in the surface Brillouin zone. The annular Majorana mode originates from the effective chiral $f$-wave superconductivity on the nonlinear Dirac cone in the former case and the interference of the effective chiral $p$-wave superconductivity on the three linear Dirac cones in the latter. In both cases, the annular Majorana mode is stabilized by the rotational symmetry and the winding number $3$ carried by the surface states. Candidate materials supporting the annular Majorana mode are predicted. Our work provides new insights into the topological superconductivity in superconducting topological insulators.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts a new type of stable Majorana zero-energy mode with a ring-shaped (annular) wave function in vortices of superconducting topological insulators that respect 3-fold or 6-fold rotational symmetry, originating from either effective chiral f-wave superconductivity on a nonlinear Dirac cone or interference of chiral p-wave superconductivity on three linear Dirac cones.
AI.motivation: To explore new topological superconducting phenomena beyond the conventional exponentially-decaying point-like Majorana zero modes in vortex cores, and to show that rotational symmetry combined with winding number 3 can stabilize a qualitatively different annular Majorana mode.
AI.method: The authors analyze superconducting vortices in topological insulators with 3-fold or 6-fold rotational symmetry, considering surface states with either a single nonlinear Dirac cone at Γ or three linear Dirac cones at M̅, and derive the annular Majorana mode from effective chiral f-wave superconductivity or interference of chiral p-wave superconductivity, respectively, stabilized by rotational symmetry and winding number 3.
AI.result: Stable annular (ring-shaped) Majorana zero-energy modes are predicted in superconducting topological insulator vortices with 3-fold or 6-fold rotational symmetry, and candidate materials are identified.
AI.conclusion: This work reveals a new class of Majorana modes with annular spatial structure, providing new insights into topological superconductivity in superconducting topological insulators.

title: Physics-Based Molecular Fingerprints from Spectral Graph Theory Provide Efficient Geometry-Aware Measures of Chemical Similarity
summary: Molecular representations are essential for the evaluation of molecular similarity and the development of structure-property relationships. Despite the known importance of 3D structure to determine chemical and physical properties, the most widely used molecular fingerprints encode only two-dimensional connectivity. Such representations fail to distinguish similar but distinct stereoisomers and conformers. Alternative 3D methods are typically defined pairwise, making their application to large chemical spaces prohibitive, while deep learning embeddings are expressive but uninterpretable and limited by their training data diversity. Here, we introduce novel physics-inspired molecular fingerprints based on principles from spectral graph theory. We represent molecules as a complete graph in 3D space, with edge weights encoding heuristic physical interactions. Eigenvalue decomposition of the resulting graph Laplacian matrix results in a computationally efficient fixed-length chemical fingerprint that encodes 3D structure while obeying necessary physical symmetries of permutation and E(3) invariance. Spectral fingerprints differentiate between unique molecular structures with identical 2D connectivity, overcoming a limitation of 2D descriptors, while maintaining the low computational cost needed for efficient screening of vast chemical spaces. We evaluate our fingerprints with community detection algorithms and observe strong performance against representative baselines across datasets from organic, inorganic, biological, reticular, and reaction chemistry. Nearest-neighbor property estimation and applicability domain analyses reveal the utility of our molecular representation in machine learning and cheminformatics. We anticipate that spectral fingerprints will serve as generalizable, interpretable, and efficient measures of chemical similarity that incorporate 3D information at minimal cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces spectral molecular fingerprints based on spectral graph theory, representing molecules as complete 3D graphs with physics-inspired edge weights. Eigenvalue decomposition of the graph Laplacian yields a fixed-length, computationally efficient fingerprint that encodes 3D structure while maintaining E(3) and permutation invariance. These fingerprints distinguish stereoisomers and conformers that 2D fingerprints cannot, while retaining screening efficiency. The method demonstrates strong performance across organic, inorganic, biological, reticular, and reaction chemistry datasets.
AI.motivation: Current molecular fingerprints are limited: 2D connectivity-based fingerprints fail to distinguish stereoisomers and conformers, pairwise 3D methods are computationally prohibitive for large chemical spaces, and deep learning embeddings are uninterpretable and constrained by training data diversity. There is a need for a 3D-aware, interpretable, and computationally efficient molecular representation.
AI.method: Molecules are represented as complete graphs in 3D space with edge weights encoding heuristic physical interactions. Eigenvalue decomposition is applied to the resulting graph Laplacian matrix to produce a fixed-length spectral fingerprint. The method leverages spectral graph theory to encode 3D structure while satisfying permutation and E(3) invariance symmetries.
AI.result: The spectral fingerprints differentiate between molecules with identical 2D connectivity, overcoming 2D descriptor limitations. Evaluation with community detection algorithms shows strong performance against representative baselines across datasets from organic, inorganic, biological, reticular, and reaction chemistry. Nearest-neighbor property estimation and applicability domain analyses demonstrate utility in machine learning and cheminformatics.
AI.conclusion: Spectral fingerprints serve as generalizable, interpretable, and efficient measures of chemical similarity that incorporate 3D structural information at minimal computational cost, offering a compelling alternative to both 2D fingerprints and deep learning embeddings.

title: Entangling power of neural networks
summary: Characterizing the complexity of correlations between subsystems is a fundamental task across information theory, machine learning, and science. In quantum physics, neural networks have found increasing application in learning wavefunctions. Here we introduce the entangling power of an encoder-decoder neural network, which quantifies its ability to generate entanglement between subsystems, dependent on a latent space dimension $K$ and the complexity class of the decoder. We exactly calculate this quantity for polynomial decoders of degree $p$ acting on a $K$-dimensional latent space. Our results establish the exponential entangling power of neural networks with modest resources. More broadly, our work provides a framework for analyzing correlations in machine learning that generalizes the notion of the Schmidt rank in entanglement theory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of "entangling power" for encoder-decoder neural networks, quantifying their ability to generate entanglement between subsystems as a function of latent space dimension K and decoder complexity class. The authors exactly compute this quantity for polynomial decoders of degree p, demonstrating exponential entangling power with modest resources, and providing a framework that generalizes Schmidt rank from entanglement theory to machine learning.
AI.motivation: Characterizing the complexity of correlations between subsystems is a fundamental task across information theory, machine learning, and science. In quantum physics, neural networks are increasingly used to learn wavefunctions, yet there is no systematic way to quantify how much entanglement such networks can actually generate.
AI.method: The authors define the entangling power of an encoder-decoder neural network as a function of the latent space dimension K and the complexity class of the decoder. They derive exact analytical calculations of this quantity for polynomial decoders of degree p acting on a K-dimensional latent space.
AI.result: The results establish that neural networks with modest resources (small latent dimension and low polynomial degree) exhibit exponential entangling power, meaning the number of Schmidt terms grows exponentially with system size.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a general framework for analyzing correlations in machine learning that generalizes the notion of Schmidt rank in entanglement theory, offering insights into the expressive power of neural networks for quantum state learning.

title: Electrically Tunable Valley-Based Qubits in Moiré Quantum Dots
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; includes 4-page Supplemental Material with 1 figure
summary: The search for scalable, electrically controlled qubits remains a central challenge in quantum technology. We introduce gate-defined moiré quantum dots as a promising platform for valley-based qubits. Moiré engineering resolves the central conflict of valley physics: momentum-space separation protects the states, while the enlarged moiré length scale allows smooth gates to mix them controllably. Dot geometry and confinement strength program valley hybridization, while a displacement field controls detuning, providing two noncommuting electrostatic axes for qubit control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces gate-defined moiré quantum dots as a novel platform for valley-based qubits in quantum technology. Moiré engineering resolves the conflict between valley state protection (via momentum-space separation) and controllable mixing (via enlarged moiré length scale enabling smooth gates). Two noncommuting electrostatic axes—dot geometry/confinement for valley hybridization and displacement field for detuning—provide qubit control.
AI.motivation: Scalable, electrically controlled qubits remain a central challenge in quantum technology. The authors aim to address this by proposing a new platform that overcomes the fundamental tension in valley qubit physics: valley states are protected by momentum-space separation, but this same separation makes them difficult to controllably mix and manipulate.
AI.method: The method introduces gate-defined moiré quantum dots as the qubit platform. Moiré engineering creates an enlarged length scale that reconciles valley state protection with controllable mixing via smooth gates. Dot geometry and confinement strength are used to program valley hybridization, while a displacement field controls detuning, yielding two noncommuting electrostatic control axes.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that moiré quantum dots provide two noncommuting electrostatic control axes (valley hybridization via geometry/confinement, and detuning via displacement field), enabling full electrostatic control of valley-based qubits.
AI.conclusion: Gate-defined moiré quantum dots constitute a promising scalable platform for electrically controlled valley-based qubits, leveraging moiré engineering to resolve the valley protection-versus-manipulation conflict.

title: Cooperative adsorption and diffusion trapping induced by AlF3 intercalation in graphite
summary: Graphite's structural and electronic response to molecular intercalation is central to its performance as a carbon-based electrode material, yet the microscopic coupling between subsurface intercalation and surface adsorption remains poorly understood. We present a first-principles investigation of AlF3 adsorption and intercalation in graphite to explain the microscopic origin of a recently observed two-step self-limiting sorption mechanism. Using density functional theory (DFT-D3), we show that a single intercalated AlF3 molecule locally transforms the structure, electronic properties, and diffusion behavior of graphite through a blister-like surface deformation. Comparing pristine graphite with a graphite surface containing a subsurface intercalated molecule, coverage-dependent adsorption energetics reveal a crossover from repulsive lateral interactions to cooperative binding above the blister, driven by local curvature and intercalation-induced charge redistribution. Diffusion-barrier calculations show that the blister simultaneously acts as a kinetic trap, raising diffusion barriers and transitioning surface mobility from a quasi-barrierless to a thermally activated regime. Charge-density difference and Mulliken population analyses identify the intercalant as a stable electronic reservoir that deepens the surface potential landscape, kinetically immobilizing adsorbed species. Together, these results establish a structure-property relationship for intercalation-induced deformation in graphite, offering a quantitative framework for controlling intercalation efficiency in carbon-based energy storage and conversion systems.

AI.tldr: First-principles DFT-D3 study reveals that a single intercalated AlF3 molecule in graphite induces a blister-like surface deformation that locally alters structural, electronic, and kinetic properties, leading to a two-step self-limiting sorption mechanism through cooperative adsorption and kinetic trapping.
AI.motivation: The microscopic coupling between subsurface intercalation and surface adsorption in graphite remains poorly understood, yet it is central to graphite's performance as a carbon-based electrode material—motivating a first-principles investigation to explain the origin of a recently observed two-step self-limiting sorption mechanism.
AI.method: Density functional theory with D3 dispersion corrections (DFT-D3) was used to study AlF3 adsorption and intercalation in graphite. The approach includes coverage-dependent adsorption energetics comparing pristine vs. intercalated graphite surfaces, diffusion-barrier calculations, charge-density difference analysis, and Mulliken population analysis.
AI.result: A single intercalated AlF3 molecule creates a blister-like surface deformation that (1) switches lateral adsorbate interactions from repulsive to cooperative above the blister due to local curvature and charge redistribution, (2) raises diffusion barriers, transitioning surface mobility from quasi-barrierless to thermally activated, and (3) acts as a stable electronic reservoir that deepens the surface potential and kinetically immobilizes adsorbed species.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a structure-property relationship for intercalation-induced deformation in graphite, providing a quantitative framework for controlling intercalation efficiency in carbon-based energy storage and conversion systems.

title: Nucleation beyond Equilibrium: Fronts Control Invasion in Bistable Ecosystems
summary: Bistability, the existence of two alternative stable states with distinct basins of attraction, is common across ecology and many other biological, chemical, and physical systems. In spatially extended systems, the invasion of one state by the other proceeds through nucleation, the fluctuation-driven growth of a droplet beyond a critical size. Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT) quantifies this process using the energy landscape, but this description relies on detailed balance, the condition of microscopic reversibility that holds at equilibrium. Ecological dynamics generally violate detailed balance and are described not by a single scalar field but by several coupled, non-conserved abundances--a vector order parameter--for which no general nucleation theory exists. Here we derive such a theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, valid both close to the binodal, where invasion proceeds through propagating fronts, and close to the spinodal, where the metastable state loses stability. Extensive numerical computations of the quasipotential confirm the theory in both regimes. We show that the mathematical structure of CNT survives out of equilibrium, once energetic quantities are replaced by dynamical properties of fronts: the front speed plays the role of the bulk free-energy difference between phases, and the diffusivity that of the surface tension. Applied to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model, an archetypal system of bistable ecological antagonism, our theory shows that strong interspecific competition generates a pronounced depletion region within fronts, where the total abundance falls well below carrying capacity. This vectorial structure, invisible to a scalar description based on species frequency alone, makes invasion exponentially harder as competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage--a prediction testable in microbial systems.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a general theory of nucleation for bistable reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, extending Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT) beyond equilibrium. The theory replaces energetic quantities with dynamical properties of fronts—front speed substitutes for bulk free-energy difference and diffusivity for surface tension—and is validated via extensive quasipotential computations. Applied to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model, it reveals that strong interspecific competition creates a depletion region within fronts that makes invasion exponentially harder, a prediction testable in microbial systems.
AI.motivation: Classical Nucleation Theory relies on detailed balance (microscopic reversibility at equilibrium), but ecological dynamics generally violate this condition and involve multiple coupled, non-conserved abundances (a vector order parameter), for which no general nucleation theory exists.
AI.method: The authors derive a nucleation theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, valid both near the binodal (invasion via propagating fronts) and near the spinodal (where the metastable state loses stability). They map energetic quantities of CNT onto dynamical front properties (front speed for bulk free-energy difference, diffusivity for surface tension) and validate the theory through extensive numerical computations of the quasipotential. They apply it to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model.
AI.result: The theory confirms the mathematical structure of CNT survives out of equilibrium after substituting energetic quantities with dynamical properties. In the Lotka-Volterra model, strong interspecific competition produces a pronounced depletion region within fronts where total abundance falls well below carrying capacity. This vectorial structure makes invasion exponentially harder as competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage.
AI.conclusion: A general nucleation theory for out-of-equilibrium, multi-species ecological systems is established, demonstrating the robustness of CNT's structure beyond equilibrium and yielding a novel, testable prediction about how interspecific competition hinders invasion in microbial systems.

title: A platform for nuclear symmetry-violation searches with laser-coolable molecules carrying spinful nuclei
summary: Cold heavy molecules are promising systems for exploring nuclear $\mathcal{P}$- and $\mathcal{CP}$-violating phenomena in search of new physics beyond the Standard Model. However, most proposed experimental strategies and their early realizations to date have been limited to proof-of-principle molecular species with effectively spin-zero nuclei that are not sensitive to nuclear symmetry-violating phenomena. Here, we introduce a comprehensive experimental toolbox that integrates cooling, trapping, coherent state manipulation, and a complete precision-measurement protocol that is applicable to molecules carrying relevant nuclear spins. Using ${}^{137}$Ba${}^{19}$F and nuclear-spin-dependent parity violation (NSD-PV) as representative species and benchmark application, respectively, our approach achieves a projected statistical sensitivity roughly two orders of magnitude beyond comparable molecular beams by combining techniques already demonstrated individually in current experiments. This level of precision could provide realistic experimental access not only to the enhanced NSD-PV signals arising from the heavy ${}^{137}$Ba nucleus within this molecule but also to the contributions from the lighter ${}^{19}$F nucleus, bringing direct benchmarks of nuclear \textit{ab initio} theory within reach. We further identify a candidate magic wavelength as a route to second-scale rotational coherence in future experiments. The techniques developed here can be transferred to measurements of nuclear Schiff and magnetic quadrupole moments in molecules containing deformed nuclei, establishing a general platform for laboratory searches for nuclear symmetry violations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive experimental toolbox combining cooling, trapping, coherent state manipulation, and a precision-measurement protocol for cold heavy molecules with nuclear spins, using 137Ba19F to achieve projected statistical sensitivity roughly two orders of magnitude beyond comparable molecular beams for nuclear-spin-dependent parity violation searches.
AI.motivation: Cold heavy molecules are promising for probing nuclear P- and CP-violating physics beyond the Standard Model, but existing strategies are limited to proof-of-principle species with effectively spin-zero nuclei, which are insensitive to nuclear symmetry-violating phenomena. A platform applicable to molecules with relevant nuclear spins is needed.
AI.method: The approach integrates cooling, trapping, coherent state manipulation, and a complete precision-measurement protocol. Using 137Ba19F as a representative species and NSD-PV as benchmark, it combines techniques already demonstrated individually in current experiments. A candidate magic wavelength is identified for achieving second-scale rotational coherence.
AI.result: The approach achieves projected statistical sensitivity roughly two orders of magnitude beyond comparable molecular beams, providing access to enhanced NSD-PV signals from the heavy 137Ba nucleus and contributions from the lighter 19F nucleus, bringing direct benchmarks of nuclear ab initio theory within reach.
AI.conclusion: The techniques can be transferred to measurements of nuclear Schiff and magnetic quadrupole moments in molecules with deformed nuclei, establishing a general platform for laboratory searches for nuclear symmetry violations beyond the Standard Model.

title: Next Generation of Ultra-Coarse-Graining: Self-Consistent Inference of Critical Internal States
summary: Bottom-up coarse-graining expands the length and time scales accessible to molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, but information loss can hinder accurate representation of multistate phenomena in complex biomolecular dynamics. Ultra-Coarse-Graining (UCG) projects discrete "quantum-like" extended degrees of freedom, or "internal states," onto coarse-grained (CG) molecules, extending CG model expressiveness. The rapid-local-equilibrium (RLE) approximation in UCG depends on user-defined collective variables (CVs, e.g., local density) and neglects correlations between internal states within and between CG molecules. We present Self-Consistent UCG (SC-UCG), which uses the underlying UCG interactions directly to assign internal states without designing CVs in the CG ensemble. During simulation, internal state probabilities are determined self-consistently through graph message passing. We enhance the RLE Hamiltonian with the Bethe approximation and AI-based inference to represent explicit correlations between UCG beads. For force-field training, we develop Multilayer Internal State Consistency (MISC), a machine-learning method derived from relative entropy minimization that avoids iterative sampling of intermediate force fields. We apply SC-UCG to a tetramer exhibiting a second-order symmetry-breaking phase transition from a supercritical racemic fluid to subcritical D-rich and L-rich fluids. SC-UCG captures collective switching of internal states in the subcritical region and recapitulates the phase transition across temperatures, despite being trained on a single-temperature dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Self-Consistent Ultra-Coarse-Graining (SC-UCG), a novel coarse-graining method that self-consistently assigns internal states to CG beads using graph message passing during simulation, enhanced with Bethe approximation and AI-based inference to capture correlations between internal states. It also introduces MISC, a machine-learning force-field training method derived from relative entropy minimization. SC-UCG successfully captures collective state switching and a symmetry-breaking phase transition in a tetramer system despite single-temperature training.
AI.motivation: Traditional bottom-up coarse-graining suffers from information loss that hinders accurate representation of multistate phenomena in complex biomolecular dynamics. Existing UCG methods with the RLE approximation rely on user-defined collective variables and neglect correlations between internal states within and between CG molecules, limiting their expressiveness and accuracy.
AI.method: SC-UCG assigns internal states without designing CVs by using underlying UCG interactions directly and determining internal state probabilities self-consistently through graph message passing during simulation. The RLE Hamiltonian is enhanced with the Bethe approximation and AI-based inference to capture explicit correlations between UCG beads. Force-field training uses MISC, a machine-learning method derived from relative entropy minimization that avoids iterative sampling of intermediate force fields.
AI.result: Applied to a tetramer exhibiting a second-order symmetry-breaking phase transition (supercritical racemic fluid to subcritical D-rich and L-rich fluids), SC-UCG captures collective switching of internal states in the subcritical region and recapitulates the phase transition across temperatures, despite being trained on a single-temperature dataset.
AI.conclusion: SC-UCG overcomes the limitations of RLE-based UCG by eliminating the need for user-defined CVs and capturing inter-bead internal state correlations, enabling accurate multistate, multiphase modeling in coarse-grained simulations with enhanced training efficiency.

title: Neural Flux Attachment: From Bose Condensates to Chiral Topological Matter
summary: Can one neural wave function describe both a Bose condensate and a chiral topological liquid? We introduce ChernFormer, which combines a fermionic transformer with a fixed Chern-Simons phase that attaches one statistical vortex to every particle pair. Each factor changes sign under exchange, so their product is exactly bosonic. The fixed phase changes statistics but not probability, making every bosonic learning problem equivalent to a fermionic one with the same approximation error and overlap. With enough capacity, ChernFormer can approximate any normalizable bosonic wave function on the plane at fixed particle number. A finite, smooth network still vanishes when particles meet, yet this contact hole can shrink while the wave function and condensate fraction approach those of a nodeless condensate. Following the needle-in-a-haystack target-reconstruction benchmark introduced in \cite{NazaryanGaggioliTengFu2025}, we test ChernFormer on the Kalmeyer--Laughlin ground state and its first two chiral edge states. The overlap curves stay close to unity through their largest sampled sizes, while independent amplitude and phase maps at $N=20$ for all three states recover both local Laughlin vortices and the collective edge vortex. By contrast, a continuous, nonzero product of identical particle-wise factors misses these elementary edge sectors. ChernFormer therefore provides one variational language for conventional bosonic order and chiral topological matter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ChernFormer, a neural network architecture combining a fermionic transformer with a fixed Chern-Simons phase that attaches statistical vortices to particle pairs, making the product exactly bosonic. This enables a single variational wave function to describe both conventional Bose condensates and chiral topological liquids like the Kalmeyer-Laughlin state, achieving high overlap with ground and edge states.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified neural wave function ansatz capable of describing both conventional bosonic order (Bose condensates) and chiral topological matter (chiral topological liquids), which are typically described by very different variational approaches.
AI.method: ChernFormer combines a fermionic transformer with a fixed Chern-Simons phase that attaches one statistical vortex to every particle pair. Each factor changes sign under particle exchange, so their product is exactly bosonic. The fixed phase changes statistics but not probability, mapping every bosonic learning problem to a fermionic one with the same approximation error and overlap.
AI.result: Testing on the Kalmeyer-Laughlin ground state and its first two chiral edge states, overlap curves remain close to unity through largest sampled sizes. Independent amplitude and phase maps at N=20 recover both local Laughlin vortices and the collective edge vortex. By contrast, a continuous nonzero product of identical particle-wise factors misses these elementary edge sectors.
AI.conclusion: ChernFormer provides a single variational language for both conventional bosonic order and chiral topological matter, demonstrating that with sufficient capacity it can approximate any normalizable bosonic wave function on the plane at fixed particle number.

title: Self-dual $S_3$ gauge theory in 2+1d: lattice model and topological phase transitions
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 18 pages of supplementary materials
summary: Electric-magnetic self-duality of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory, realized microscopically as a half-lattice-translation exchanging electric charge and magnetic flux, has been an influential example of a duality symmetry with an exact lattice realization. We construct the first non-Abelian generalization of this construction: a lattice model of the $S_3$ quantum double $\mathcal{D}(S_3)$ on a tensor product Hilbert space in which the $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{em}}_2$ anyon-permutation symmetry, exchanging the non-Abelian chargeon $C$ and fluxon $F$, is realized via lattice translation. Consequently we find that the zigzag boundary termination of the model realizes, without fine-tuning, a gapless critical edge state described by the tetracritical Ising CFT. The bulk admits three independent $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\mathrm{em}}$-preserving bosonic perturbations, driving $\mathcal{D}(S_3)$ into distinct gapped phases. We analyze these transitions by three independent methods: category-theoretic anyon condensation, microscopic lattice Hamiltonians, and Chern-Simons-Higgs theory, which all agree, yielding a unified picture. These examples motivate a minimal-condensation principle: proliferating a bosonic anyon generically drives condensation of a minimal condensable algebra containing it, with symmetry-related condensates appearing as degenerate vacua that spontaneously break the anyon-permutation symmetry. Our model construction extends to an infinite family of self-dual dihedral quantum doubles $\mathcal{D}(D_{2n})$. Notably, each model is sign-problem-free, opening the door to large-scale numerical exploration of the phases of non-Abelian Chern-Simons-Higgs theories.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs the first non-Abelian generalization of the electric-magnetic self-dual Z2 gauge theory: a lattice model of the S3 quantum double D(S3) where the Z2 anyon-permutation symmetry (exchanging the non-Abelian chargeon C and fluxon F) is realized via lattice translation. The zigzag boundary yields a gapless tetracritical Ising CFT edge state without fine-tuning, and the bulk has three independent Z2-preserving perturbations leading to distinct gapped phases, analyzed consistently via anyon condensation, microscopic lattice Hamiltonians, and Chern-Simons-Higgs theory. The work generalizes to an infinite family of self-dual dihedral quantum doubles D(D2n), all sign-problem-free.
AI.motivation: The electric-magnetic self-duality of Z2 gauge theory, realized via half-lattice translation, is a foundational example of a duality symmetry with an exact lattice realization. The authors aim to generalize this construction to non-Abelian anyonic systems, which is significantly more complex and has not been achieved before. They seek to construct lattice models with anyon-permutation symmetries realized as lattice translations, and to understand the resulting boundary physics and phase structure.
AI.method: The authors construct a lattice model of the S3 quantum double D(S3) on a tensor product Hilbert space in which the Z2_em anyon-permutation symmetry (exchanging the non-Abelian chargeon C and fluxon F) is realized as a lattice translation. They analyze the phase transitions driven by three independent Z2_em-preserving bosonic perturbations using three independent methods: category-theoretic anyon condensation, microscopic lattice Hamiltonians, and Chern-Simons-Higgs theory. The model construction extends to an infinite family of self-dual dihedral quantum doubles D(D2n).
AI.result: The zigzag boundary termination of the model realizes, without fine-tuning, a gapless critical edge state described by the tetracritical Ising CFT. The bulk admits three independent Z2_em-preserving bosonic perturbations driving D(S3) into distinct gapped phases, and all three analysis methods (anyon condensation, microscopic lattice Hamiltonians, Chern-Simons-Higgs theory) agree, yielding a unified picture. The work motivates a minimal-condensation principle: proliferating a bosonic anyon generically drives condensation of a minimal condensable algebra containing it, with symmetry-related condensates appearing as degenerate vacua spontaneously breaking the anyon-permutation symmetry. The construction extends to an infinite family of self-dual dihedral quantum doubles, all sign-problem-free.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a general framework for realizing non-Abelian anyon-permutation symmetries via lattice translations, demonstrates that such constructions yield non-trivial gapless boundary states (tetracritical Ising CFT) without fine-tuning, and reveals a minimal-condensation principle governing the phase transitions. The sign-problem-free nature of these models opens the door to large-scale numerical exploration of non-Abelian Chern-Simons-Higgs theories, potentially enabling deeper understanding of symmetry-enriched topological phases and their transitions.

title: Simulation of positronium laser cooling using the Lindblad master equation
summary: We present a formulation and numerical results for positronium (Ps) laser cooling. The formulation is based on the Lindblad master equation and follows the time evolution of the density matrix of Ps atoms. It therefore accounts for atomic coherence, which is necessary to describe the interaction of Ps with the train of short laser pulses generated by the system developed by Shu $\textit{et al.}$ [K. Shu $\textit{et al.}$, Phys. Rev. A $\textbf{109}$, 043520 (2024)]. We present the representative time evolution of the internal-state populations and momentum distribution, together with a comprehensive scan of the laser parameters used to optimize the cooling efficiency. A prominent feature of the simulated distributions is sub-recoil cooling through velocity-selective coherent population trapping, a coherent effect captured by the quantum-mechanical treatment.

title: X-ray Driven Trihydrogen Formation on Silica Nanosurfaces
summary: The trihydrogen cation ($\mathrm{H_3^+}$) initiates the ion-molecule reactions that build molecular complexity in interstellar space. Whether its canonical formation reaction, $\mathrm{H_2^+ + H_2 \rightarrow H_3^+ + H}$, proceeds on inorganic surfaces under radiation-driven ionization has remained untested. Here we drive $\mathrm{H_3^+}$ formation on hydrated silica nanoparticles using intense 1.88 keV X-ray pulses, combining ion velocity map imaging, electron time-of-flight spectroscopy, and single-particle coherent diffractive imaging to resolve this chemistry on individual particles. The self-induced surface electric field on the V/nm scale drives interfacial charge transfer and water fragmentation. This field is the dominant parameter governing the relative yields of $\mathrm{H^+}$, $\mathrm{H_2^+}$, and $\mathrm{H_3^+}$ across particle size, composition, and aggregation. Density functional theory and nonadiabatic quantum molecular dynamics simulations trace this field-driven charge transfer, directly analogous to band bending at semiconductor photoelectrodes. These results establish surface-field-driven charge transfer as a unifying mechanism between radiation dominated astrophysical environments and field-driven surface catalysis.

This establishes surface-field-driven charge transfer as a unifying mechanism linking astrophysical radiation chemistry and field-driven surface catalysis.

title: Dual-Faraday-laser-pumped cesium beam clock with $7.7\times 10^{-13}/\sqrtτ$ frequency stability
summary: Compact cesium beam clocks are major frequency references for deployable timing systems. However, further improvement of their short-term frequency stability is limited by the clock signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Although two-laser optical pumping can increase the effective atomic utilization, the achievable clock SNR has long been limited by laser-induced frequency-to-amplitude noise conversion. Here, we demonstrate a compact dual-Faraday-laser-pumped (DFP) Cs beam clock enabled by a low-frequency-noise atom-referenced laser architecture. The intracavity Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter provides inherent alignment to the Cs D$_2$ resonances, while modulation transfer spectroscopy offers suppressed frequency noise and drift. The resulting laser system supports robust turnkey operation with a Lorentzian linewidth of 2.12 kHz. The DFP Cs clock achieves a clock SNR of 46,365 in a 1-Hz bandwidth and a fractional Allan deviation of $7.7\times 10^{-13}/\sqrtτ$ , with Hadamard deviation reaching $7.7\times 10^{-15}$ at 10,000 s. This work pushes the fractional frequency stability of a compact Cs beam clock into the $10^{-13}/\sqrtτ$ regime, providing a pathway toward high-performance Cs frequency references for field-deployable precision timing, navigation, and synchronization.

By using a low-frequency-noise atom-referenced laser with intracavity Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filtering and modulation transfer spectroscopy, the clock achieves a SNR of 46,365 in 1-Hz bandwidth, fractional Allan deviation of 7.7×10⁻¹³/√τ, and Hadamard deviation of 7.7×10⁻¹⁵ at 10,000 s—pushing compact Cs beam clocks into the 10⁻¹³/√τ stability regime for field-deployable timing applications.

While two-laser optical pumping can improve atomic utilization efficiency, the achievable clock SNR has been constrained by laser-induced frequency-to-amplitude noise conversion, preventing further stability improvements.

This laser system employs an intracavity Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter that inherently aligns the laser to Cs D₂ resonances and modulation transfer spectroscopy to suppress frequency noise and drift. title: One-dimensional Dirac modes in the core of a pentagonal topological crystalline insulator nanowire
summary: We investigate the electronic band topology of recently fabricated pentagonal IV-VI semiconductor nanowires, which contain five radial $\{111\}$ twin planes meeting at the nanowire axis. Tight-binding calculations show that, when the bulk band structure is inverted and the twin planes in the nanowire are cationic, the spectrum contains two spatially separated helical Dirac crossings near $\overlineΓ$: one localized at the core and the other at the outer surface. When the twin planes are anionic, the corresponding spectra remain gapped. The crossings originate from the hybridization of five helical channels associated with the twin-plane edges, whose odd number leaves one Kramers pair near the nanowire axis and the other at the outer boundary. Realistic multiorbital calculations for $\mathrm{Pb}_{0.4}\mathrm{Sn}_{0.6}\mathrm{Te}$ predict well-developed core and surface modes at nanowire thicknesses of approximately 50~nm and above. These results establish pentagonal SnTe-class nanowires as an experimentally accessible realization of spatially separated helical channels bound to the axial defect and the outer boundary.

Tight-binding and multiorbital calculations show that when the bulk band structure is inverted and twin planes are cationic, two spatially separated helical Dirac crossings emerge—one at the nanowire core and one at the outer surface—arising from hybridization of five helical channels whose odd number places one Kramers pair at the axis and another at the boundary. Anionic twin planes leave the spectrum gapped. These nanowires provide an experimentally accessible realization of spatially separated helical channels bound to the axial defect and outer boundary.
AI.motivation: To determine whether recently fabricated pentagonal IV-VI semiconductor nanowires—containing multiple twin planes—can host spatially separated helical topological states, and to establish them as an experimentally accessible platform for such exotic band topology.
AI.method: Tight-binding calculations of electronic band topology, supported by realistic multiorbital calculations for Pb₀.₄Sn₀.₆Te, analyzing the effect of cationic vs. anionic twin planes on the nanowire spectrum and tracing the topological origin of helical crossings to hybridization of an odd number of helical channels from twin-plane edges.

Anionic twin planes keep the spectrum gapped. The crossings are attributed to hybridization of five helical channels, whose odd count yields one Kramers pair at the axis and one at the boundary. Multiorbital calculations for Pb₀.₄Sn₀.₆Te predict well-developed core and surface modes at nanowire thicknesses of ~50 nm and above.

title: Local Spin Excitations Mediate Quasiparticle Breakdown in the Orbital-Selective Mott Phase
summary: The orbital-selective Mott phase (OSMP) is commonly described as a coexistence of localized and itinerant electrons within effectively decoupled orbitals, but emerging evidence for quasiparticle breakdown points to physics beyond this picture, whose microscopic origin remains unknown. Using dynamical mean-field theory for the two-band Hubbard model, we show that the spin-flip and Ising-type components of Hund's coupling generate local spin excitations (LSEs). These LSEs couple electrons between different orbitals, renormalize quasiparticle lifetimes and binding energies, and thereby destroy well-defined quasiparticles in the OSMP. Removing these two components of Hund's coupling restores coherent quasiparticle behavior and fully decouples the charge dynamics of the two bands. Our results therefore identify electronic coupling to LSEs as the fundamental mechanism driving quasiparticle breakdown within the OSMP.

Removing these coupling components restores coherent quasiparticles and decouples the two bands' charge dynamics, identifying LSE coupling as the fundamental mechanism for quasiparticle breakdown in the OSMP.
AI.motivation: The OSMP has traditionally been described as coexisting localized and itinerant electrons in decoupled orbitals, but emerging evidence of quasiparticle breakdown suggests physics beyond this picture whose microscopic origin remains unknown.
AI.method: Dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) applied to the two-band Hubbard model, with systematic removal of specific Hund's coupling components (spin-flip and Ising-type) to isolate their role in quasiparticle dynamics.
AI.result: The spin-flip and Ising components of Hund's coupling generate local spin excitations that couple electrons between orbitals, renormalize quasiparticle lifetimes and binding energies, and destroy well-defined quasiparticles in the OSMP. Removing these components restores coherent quasiparticle behavior and decouples the charge dynamics of the two bands.
AI.conclusion: Electronic coupling to local spin excitations is identified as the fundamental mechanism driving quasiparticle breakdown within the OSMP.

title: Jsymm: A Python package for symmetry analysis of exchange tensors in magnetic Hamiltonians
summary: Symmetries of a crystal often restrict its physical properties. In particular, they determine possible forms of the tensors that describe interatomic exchange interaction, which governs a wide range of magnetic phenomena. Computationally demanding first-principles calculations of the exchange tensors can be greatly simplified by taking the symmetry constraints into account. Here, we present Jsymm, a Python package that derives the most general symmetry-compatible form of the exchange tensors directly from the crystallographic data. For any bond formed by magnetic ions, Jsymm produces the tensors of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and anisotropic Heisenberg exchange interaction in symbolic form, as well as the tensors for all other bonds related to it by symmetry. This reduces the number of independent model parameters, dramatically lowering the computational cost of the ab initio calculations and preventing unphysical results arising from symmetry violations. The package accepts standard CIF files and provides a web interface in addition to an interactive text mode and a Python library. We demonstrate its utility on La$_2$CuO$_4$ and $α$-Fe$_2$O$_3$, reproducing known symmetry constraints and revealing additional relations between components of the exchange tensors of different bonds.

AI.tldr: Jsymm is a Python package that automatically derives the most general symmetry-compatible forms of exchange tensors (Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and anisotropic Heisenberg exchange) directly from crystallographic data, reducing the number of independent model parameters and lowering computational costs for first-principles calculations.
AI.motivation: Crystal symmetries determine the allowed forms of exchange tensors governing magnetic phenomena, but incorporating these constraints into computationally demanding first-principles calculations is challenging. A tool is needed to automatically derive symmetry-compatible tensor forms to simplify calculations and prevent symmetry-violating results.
AI.method: Jsymm takes standard CIF files as input and derives the most general symmetry-compatible exchange tensor forms for any bond between magnetic ions. It produces symbolic tensors for Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and anisotropic Heisenberg exchange, including tensors for all symmetry-related bonds. The package offers multiple interfaces: a web interface, interactive text mode, and a Python library.
AI.result: The package was demonstrated on La2CuO4 and alpha-Fe2O3, successfully reproducing known symmetry constraints and revealing additional relations between components of exchange tensors of different bonds.
AI.conclusion: Jsymm dramatically reduces the number of independent model parameters in magnetic exchange models, lowering computational costs of ab initio calculations and preventing unphysical results from symmetry violations, making it a practical tool for computing exchange interactions.

title: Low-resistivity nitrogen-doped p-type Cu2O thin films enabled by millisecond flash lamp annealing
summary: Flash lamp annealing (FLA) provides millisecond-scale thermal processing, but its effects on p-type Cu2O and nitrogen-related defects remain poorly understood. Reactively sputtered Cu2O:N films with different nitrogen content were deposited using reactive high-power impulse magnetron sputtering and exposed to a single 1.9 ms FLA pulse at 4.9 - 11.7 J cm-2. Their compositional,morphological, structural, vibrational, electrical, and optical responses were evaluated. WDS showed no statistically significant change in total elemental composition, and XRD confirmed retention of cubic Cu2O. Nitrogen-containing films exhibited surface coarsening, shifts of the Cu2O reflections, and non-monotonic changes in the Raman band assigned to molecular N2. Nitrogen incorporation substantially reduced the as-deposited resistivity. The very low value of 0.045 Ωcm was obtained after FLA at 4.9 J cm-2, whereas higher energy densities markedly increased resistivity. Hall measurements showed increasing mobility but decreasing hole concentration. At high energy densities, the optical band gap of nitrogen-rich films widened. The results define a narrow low-energy processing window with a positive effect on electrical properties, whereas high-energy FLA modifies the structure and optical absorption edge but degrades electrical conductivity.

AI.tldr: This study examines the effects of flash lamp annealing (FLA) on reactively sputtered p-type Cu2O:N films. A single 1.9 ms FLA pulse at 4.9-11.7 J cm-2 was applied; low energy densities (4.9 J cm-2) improved electrical properties (resistivity down to 0.045 Ωcm), while high energy densities widened the optical band gap but degraded electrical conductivity, despite retained cubic Cu2O structure and unchanged composition.
AI.motivation: The effects of millisecond-scale flash lamp annealing on p-type Cu2O and nitrogen-related defects are poorly understood, motivating a systematic investigation of how FLA energy density influences the compositional, structural, electrical, and optical properties of nitrogen-doped Cu2O films.
AI.method: Cu2O:N films with varying nitrogen content were deposited by reactive high-power impulse magnetron sputtering (HiPIMS) and exposed to a single 1.9 ms FLA pulse at 4.9-11.7 J cm-2. Films were characterized by WDS (composition), XRD (structure), Raman spectroscopy (vibrational modes), Hall measurements (electrical), and optical absorption measurements.
AI.result: FLA did not significantly change total composition and retained cubic Cu2O. Nitrogen-containing films showed surface coarsening, shifted Cu2O reflections, and non-monotonic N2 Raman band changes. Nitrogen doping reduced as-deposited resistivity; the lowest value of 0.045 Ωcm was achieved after 4.9 J cm-2 FLA. Higher energy densities increased resistivity, with increasing mobility but decreasing hole concentration. At high energy densities, nitrogen-rich films exhibited a widened optical band gap.
AI.conclusion: A narrow low-energy FLA processing window positively affects electrical properties of Cu2O:N films, whereas high-energy FLA modifies structure and optical absorption edge but degrades electrical conductivity. This defines an energy-density-dependent trade-off for optimizing transparent p-type oxide films.

title: Morphology of frozen labyrinths from irreversible threshold dynamics
summary: Majority threshold dynamics, in which each agent adopts the dominant state in a weighted neighborhood, relaxes a binary field toward consensus or stripes. We study what happens when this rule is made irreversible: each agent, interacting through a Gaussian kernel on a lattice, may flip out of its local weighted minority at most once. The reversible form is threshold dynamics of Merriman-Bence-Osher type, an exactly solvable calibration in which interfaces move by mean curvature with closed-form lattice pinning and mobility. Irreversibility changes the outcome. From random initial conditions, the one-flip rule freezes balanced non-consensus labyrinths that reversible relaxation drives away. The patterned regime is a window of initial spin compositions around equal balance, narrowing as the interaction range grows, controlled by a standardized bias whose onset is independent of scale over a fourfold range. The frozen morphology is arrested coarsening: bicontinuous at balance, with a feature width that grows sublinearly and falls below the interaction range at large scales. We determine the mechanism by intervention. Fixing the initial condition while varying the update order shows that the coarse domain layout is deterministic, while the update order enters only in a secondary first-passage race that fine-tunes the wall positions the deterministic dynamics has already set. Those walls are marked by frustration: agents frozen against their own local field. This signature is identically absent from any reversible relaxation, is overwhelmingly interfacial, and carries almost none of the pattern's large-scale shape.

AI.tldr: The paper studies irreversible majority threshold dynamics where each agent can flip at most once, showing that this one-flip rule freezes balanced non-consensus labyrinths from random initial conditions, producing arrested coarsening patterns whose coarse layout is deterministic while update order only fine-tunes wall positions via a first-passage race.
AI.motivation: To understand how irreversibility in majority threshold dynamics (where reversible dynamics follow mean curvature motion via MBO thresholding) changes the outcome, and to characterize the frozen patterned states that arise from the one-flip constraint.
AI.method: The authors analyze a lattice model with Gaussian kernel interactions where agents may flip out of their local weighted minority at most once. They compare against reversible threshold dynamics of Merriman-Bence-Osher type, study the patterned regime as a function of initial spin composition, and determine the mechanism by fixing initial conditions while varying update order.
AI.result: The one-flip rule freezes balanced non-consensus labyrinths that reversible relaxation drives away. The patterned regime is a window of initial compositions around equal balance that narrows with interaction range, controlled by a standardized bias with scale-independent onset. Frozen morphologies show arrested coarsening with sublinear feature growth below the interaction range at large scales. The coarse domain layout is deterministic, while update order only fine-tunes wall positions via a first-passage race. Walls are marked by frustration (agents frozen against their local field), which is absent from reversible relaxation and carries little of the pattern's large-scale shape.
AI.conclusion: Irreversibility fundamentally changes majority threshold dynamics, producing frozen labyrinthine patterns through arrested coarsening. The pattern's coarse structure is deterministically determined, with update order playing only a secondary fine-tuning role, and frustration at interfaces is the hallmark signature distinguishing irreversible from reversible dynamics.

title: A Phase Space Electronic Structure View of The Solid State
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, main text and SM
summary: We develop a phase space electronic structure view of the solid state, where electronic bands are parameterized by both nuclear position $\mathbf{Q}$ and nuclear momentum $\mathbfΠ$ (rather than the standard practice of only $\mathbf{Q}$). Within this phase space, non-Born-Oppenheimer electronic structure context, we prove a nuclear wavevector ($\mathbf{q}$)-dependent version of Nafie's equality relating the change in electronic momentum as a function of nuclear momentum, $\partial \langle\mathbf{p}\rangle/\partial \mathbfΠ_q$, to the change in electronic position as a function of nuclear position, $\partial \langle\mathbf{r}\rangle/\partial \mathbf{Q}q$. Furthermore, we show how information about electron-phonon interactions, specifically nuclear-induced electronic momentum, can be extracted from simple band structure calculations -- without Berry curvature calculations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a phase space electronic structure theory for solids where electronic bands depend on both nuclear position and nuclear momentum. It proves a q-dependent version of Nafie's equality relating derivatives of electronic momentum and position, and shows how electron-phonon interaction information can be extracted from band structure calculations without Berry curvature.
AI.motivation: To extend the standard solid-state electronic structure framework beyond position-only parameterization, incorporating nuclear momentum to capture non-Born-Oppenheimer effects and establish a practical route to extracting electron-phonon coupling information.
AI.method: A phase space formulation of solid-state electronic structure where electronic bands are functions of both nuclear position Q and momentum Π. The authors prove a nuclear wavevector-dependent generalization of Nafie's equality and demonstrate how nuclear-induced electronic momentum can be obtained from standard band structure calculations.
AI.result: A q-dependent Nafie equality is proven relating ∂⟨p⟩/∂Π_q to ∂⟨r⟩/∂Q_q. It is demonstrated that electron-phonon interaction information can be extracted from band structure calculations without requiring Berry curvature computations.
AI.conclusion: Phase space electronic structure provides a fruitful framework for studying non-Born-Oppenheimer effects in solids, offering a simplified pathway to electron-phonon interaction data from conventional band structure.

title: An Effective String Theory Toolbox for Quantum Hall Interfaces I: Worldsheet Kinematics and Constraint Structure
summary: A freely moving quantum Hall interface is fundamentally different from an ordinary edge fixed by an external confining potential. Since a normal displacement changes the areas occupied by the adjacent incompressible phases, the interface geometry and charge dynamics cannot be treated as independent degrees of freedom. We formulate this problem for interfaces between Abelian quantum Hall phases using a spatially reparametrization-invariant worldsheet description, in which tangential motion is a relabeling of the interface while normal motion is physical. Starting from the two-sided Chern--Simons response, we derive the relation between normal charge transport and interface motion. We then introduce a relative-area construction, defined with respect to a material reference curve, that converts this velocity relation into an equal-time constraint linking the charged boundary sector to the interface shape. Combined with the folded $K$-matrix current algebra, this identifies the universal Hall kinematics of the moving interface while leaving its geometric energy and neutral dynamics dependent on microscopic interface physics. The resulting framework provides a systematic basis for effective theories of dynamical quantum Hall interfaces.

Using a spatially reparametrization-invariant description and a relative-area construction, the authors derive an equal-time constraint linking charge transport to interface shape, combined with the folded K-matrix current algebra to identify universal Hall kinematics while leaving geometric energy and neutral dynamics as microscopic details.
AI.motivation: Freely moving quantum Hall interfaces fundamentally differ from fixed edges defined by external confining potentials, because the interface geometry and charge dynamics are coupled degrees of freedom. A systematic theoretical framework is needed to treat such dynamical interfaces, which existing edge theories based on fixed confining potentials cannot describe.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem using a spatially reparametrization-invariant worldsheet description where tangential motion is a relabeling while normal motion is physical. They derive the velocity relation between normal charge transport and interface motion from two-sided Chern-Simons response, then introduce a relative-area construction defined with respect to a material reference curve to convert this into an equal-time constraint. This is combined with the folded K-matrix current algebra.
AI.result: The framework identifies the universal Hall kinematics of a moving quantum Hall interface, establishing the relationship between interface shape and the charged boundary sector, while showing that geometric energy and neutral dynamics depend on microscopic interface physics. This yields a systematic basis for effective theories of dynamical quantum Hall interfaces.
AI.conclusion: The authors provide a systematic framework for effective theories of dynamical quantum Hall interfaces, separating universal Hall kinematics from microscopic-dependent geometric and neutral degrees of freedom, applicable to interfaces between Abelian quantum Hall phases.

title: Antiferromagnetic Phases in Zr-Fe-Ge Kagome Systems
summary: A wide variety of chemical substitutions in ferromagnetic Kagome systems can lead to diverse magnetic phases with electronic structures suitable for topological or quantum material properties. Here, we study the electronic structure and magnetic orderings using first-principles calculations for the magnetic Kagome compounds ZrFe6Ge6, ZrFe6Ge4, and ZrFe6Ge5. For ZrFe6Ge6, the obtained ground-state magnetic structure is A-type antiferromagnetic (AFM), in agreement with existing experiments. We predicted that the magnetic ground states of ZrFe6Ge4 and ZrFe6Ge5 are collinear A-type bilayer AFM structures with long-period ordering that involves a mix of FM and AFM interlayer orientations. The formation of such long-range magnetic structures appears to be a general feature and is not tied to specific substitutions. The magnetic moments in these systems are largely local and only weakly dependent on the magnetic configuration, with magnitudes in good agreement with available experimental estimates. Neutron scattering experiments, which could provide direct verification of these predictions, are therefore of particular importance.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations of the Kagome compounds ZrFe6Ge6, ZrFe6Ge4, and ZrFe6Ge5 predict that ZrFe6Ge6 has an A-type antiferromagnetic ground state (consistent with experiments), while ZrFe6Ge4 and ZrFe6Ge5 exhibit collinear A-type bilayer AFM structures with long-period FM/AFM interlayer ordering. The magnetic moments are local and weakly configuration-dependent.
AI.motivation: Chemical substitutions in ferromagnetic Kagome systems can produce diverse magnetic phases relevant to topological and quantum materials, but the magnetic orderings in these specific ZrFe6Ge6-family compounds were not well characterized theoretically.
AI.method: First-principles (density functional theory) calculations to study electronic structures and magnetic ground-state orderings of ZrFe6Ge6, ZrFe6Ge4, and ZrFe6Ge5 Kagome compounds.
AI.result: ZrFe6Ge6 stabilizes in an A-type antiferromagnetic state matching experiments. ZrFe6Ge4 and ZrFe6Ge5 are predicted to form collinear A-type bilayer AFM structures with long-period ordering mixing FM and AFM interlayer orientations. Magnetic moments are largely local, weakly dependent on magnetic configuration, and agree with experimental estimates.
AI.conclusion: Long-range magnetic structures appear to be a general feature of these substituted Kagome systems, and neutron scattering experiments are proposed as essential direct verification of the predicted magnetic orderings.

title: Entanglement Scaling and Full Counting Statistics in Excited States of Two-Dimensional Rotating Fermions
summary: We investigate the entanglement entropy of a class of $N$-particle excited state of fermions confined in a two-dimensional harmonic trap rotating at an angular frequency $Ω$. The excited state is constructed by filling a particular set of $N$ single-particle energy levels. We analytically compute the Rényi entropies of order $q$ in a disc of radius $r$ around the centre of the trap, and the cumulants corresponding to number fluctuations of fermions within the disc. We found that the area law scaling of entanglement entropy holds even for a class of excited states. We also verified the well-known series expansion of entanglement entropy in terms of the particle number cumulants for non-interacting fermions. We further derive the centered cumulant generating function, demonstrating that the associated probability distribution function in the disc has identical scaling properties, up to a variable shift, to the known ground-state result. Finally, we extend our result to an annular region, showing that both the Rényi entropy and particle number cumulants of the annulus decompose into sums of the corresponding quantities of the two bounding discs. These additive relations hold as long as the width of the annulus is sufficiently large.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically studies entanglement entropy of N-particle excited states of fermions in a 2D rotating harmonic trap, computing Rényi entropies, number cumulants, and showing area-law scaling, cumulant expansions, and additive decompositions for annular regions.
AI.motivation: To extend the understanding of entanglement entropy from ground states to excited states of fermionic systems in 2D harmonic traps, and to verify whether known properties such as area-law scaling and cumulant expansions hold for excited states.
AI.method: Fermions occupy a chosen set of N single-particle energy levels in a 2D harmonic trap rotating at angular frequency Ω. The authors analytically compute Rényi entropies of order q in a disc of radius r, particle number cumulants within the disc, and derive the centered cumulant generating function. They extend the analysis to annular regions.
AI.result: Area-law scaling of entanglement entropy holds for this class of excited states. The cumulant series expansion of entanglement entropy is verified for non-interacting fermions. The probability distribution in the disc shows identical scaling (up to a variable shift) to the ground state. For annular regions, both Rényi entropy and cumulants decompose additively into bounding disc contributions when the annulus is sufficiently wide.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement properties of a specific class of excited states in rotating harmonic traps mirror ground-state behavior, including area-law scaling and additive decomposition for annuli, suggesting universality of these entanglement characteristics beyond ground states.

title: Nuclear-Spin Statistical Weights from Young Diagrams
summary: Nuclear-spin statistical weights and selection rules in molecular spectroscopy are governed by the permutation symmetry of identical nuclei, although rigid and semi-rigid molecules typically realize only a proper subgroup of the full symmetric group. Building on the Schur-Weyl framework of Schmiedt, Jensen, and Schlemmer, we extend this approach to molecular geometries whose rovibrational motion realizes cyclic and dihedral permutation subgroups. By combining the Schur-Weyl decomposition of the $n$-spin Hilbert space with the Kraśkiewicz-Weyman-Adin-Roichman major-index branching rule for the restriction $S_N \downarrow C_m$, we obtain a fully combinatorial method for determining nuclear-spin symmetry species and statistical weights. Each standard Young tableau corresponds to a definite cyclic character determined by its major index, with reflections yielding the associated dihedral symmetry, so that nuclear-spin species follow directly from tableau data without projection operators or case-specific constructions. The approach supplies the symmetry information required for rovibrational line-intensity modeling and provides a practical, automatable framework for nuclear-spin symmetry analysis in polyatomic molecules.
