title: An Effective String Theory Toolbox for Quantum Hall Interfaces II: Majorana Fermions on Fluctuating Moore-Read Worldsheets
summary: A Moore--Read interface carries a chiral Majorana mode on a boundary whose geometry may itself fluctuate. Fixed-edge theory does not determine how this neutral mode should be transported when the interface bends and moves, or how its dynamics couples to the fluctuating shape. Here we construct a spatially reparametrization-invariant Majorana theory on the nonrelativistic worldsheet of a freely moving interface. The changing line element fixes a universal half-density transport law, while additional curvature- and velocity-dependent couplings remain controlled by microscopic interface physics. The resulting framework identifies the Majorana stress tensor as the mediator between neutral and geometric dynamics and provides the neutral sector needed for effective theories of dynamical non-Abelian quantum Hall interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a spatially reparametrization-invariant Majorana theory on the nonrelativistic worldsheet of a freely moving interface, establishing how chiral Majorana modes transport when the boundary geometry fluctuates and identifying the Majorana stress tensor as the mediator between neutral and geometric dynamics.
AI.motivation: Fixed-edge theory does not determine how a chiral Majorana mode at a Moore-Read interface should be transported when the interface bends and moves, nor how its dynamics couples to the fluctuating interface shape. A comprehensive effective theory of dynamical non-Abelian quantum Hall interfaces requires a consistent framework for the neutral sector under geometric fluctuations.
AI.method: The authors construct a spatially reparametrization-invariant Majorana field theory on the nonrelativistic worldsheet of a freely moving interface. The changing line element fixes a universal half-density transport law, and additional curvature- and velocity-dependent couplings are parameterized, with the Majorana stress tensor serving as the mediator between neutral and geometric degrees of freedom.
AI.result: The framework yields a universal half-density transport law for the Majorana mode dictated by the metric, while curvature- and velocity-dependent couplings remain controlled by microscopic interface physics. The Majorana stress tensor is identified as the mediator coupling neutral and geometric dynamics.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the neutral sector needed for effective theories of dynamical non-Abelian quantum Hall interfaces, establishing how chiral Majorana modes behave on fluctuating interface geometries.

title: Correlated topological-polarization surface states in the narrow-gap insulator FeSb2
summary: Strong electron correlations and band topology each generate rich quantum phases, but conflicting elemental requirements have largely kept them apart. Topological polarization offers a route to unite them, producing polar surface states from bonding charge without spin-orbit coupling and thereby extending band topology to correlated 3d transition-metal compounds. Here we demonstrate that epitaxial thin films of the narrow-gap insulator FeSb2 host metallic polar surface states of topological-polarization origin, governed by the strong correlations of the bulk. Nonreciprocal surface transport emerges only below the onset temperature of a correlation-driven reconstruction of the bulk Fe 3d orbital occupation, providing direct evidence of bulk-edge correspondence in a correlated topological system. Moreover, electrostatic gating drives this correlated surface across a quantum phase transition into a ferromagnetic or possibly altermagnetic state. Our results establish topological polarization as a design principle for correlated topological phases in a broad range of materials.

AI.tldr: Epitaxial thin films of the correlated narrow-gap insulator FeSb2 exhibit metallic polar surface states arising from topological polarization, with nonreciprocal surface transport tied to a bulk correlation-driven orbital reconstruction—demonstrating bulk-edge correspondence in a correlated topological system and enabling electrostatic gating to drive the surface into a ferromagnetic or altermagnetic state.
AI.motivation: Strong electron correlations and band topology rarely coexist because their elemental requirements conflict. The authors aim to use topological polarization—which generates polar surface states from bonding charge without spin-orbit coupling—as a route to unify these phenomena and extend band topology into correlated 3d transition-metal compounds.
AI.method: The authors grow epitaxial thin films of FeSb2, a narrow-gap correlated insulator, and probe its surface states and transport properties. They measure nonreciprocal surface transport as a function of temperature, track bulk Fe 3d orbital occupation changes via correlation-driven reconstruction, and apply electrostatic gating to control the correlated surface electronic state.
AI.result: The films host metallic polar surface states of topological-polarization origin governed by bulk correlations. Nonreciprocal surface transport emerges only below the onset of a bulk correlation-driven Fe 3d orbital reconstruction, giving direct evidence of bulk-edge correspondence. Electrostatic gating drives the correlated surface across a quantum phase transition into a ferromagnetic or possibly altermagnetic state.
AI.conclusion: Topological polarization is established as a design principle for realizing correlated topological phases, connecting bulk strong correlations to surface topological transport in materials such as FeSb2.

title: Intra-unit-cell resolved intertwining of multi-$Q$ charge and spin textures in an itinerant skyrmion magnet
summary: The mechanisms stabilizing non-collinear magnetism in centrosymmetric crystals remain unclear, but likely involve spin-spin interactions mediated by itinerant electrons, such as the RKKY interaction. Finite-$Q$ magnetic order may then be accompanied by electronic modulations that are observable using a scanning tunneling microscope. In five successive magnetic phases of GdRu$_{2}$Ge$_{2}$, including two nano-scale skyrmion crystal phases, we show that multi-$Q$ magnetism among Gd 4$f$ spins entails a corresponding multi-$Q$ texture among the Ru 4$d$ orbitals that contribute itinerant electron bands. With atomically-resolved images of each electronic texture's motif, and a simple numerical modeling scheme drawing on the underlying spin structures, we infer their key relationship: The alignment between nearest-neighbor Gd spins tightly correlates with the local density-of-states of the Ru 4$d$ orbitals on the two bond-centered sublattices of the Gd square net. These analyses offer a microscopic view of the atomic-scale intertwining of charge and spin degrees-of-freedom in non-collinear itinerant magnets.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the coupling between non-collinear magnetism and electronic textures in GdRu2Ge2. Using atomically-resolved STM imaging across five magnetic phases (including two skyrmion crystal phases), the authors show that multi-Q magnetic order among Gd 4f spins generates corresponding multi-Q electronic textures among Ru 4d orbitals. A simple numerical model reveals that nearest-neighbor Gd spin alignment strongly correlates with the local density-of-states on bond-centered Ru sublattices, providing microscopic insight into charge-spin intertwining in itinerant non-collinear magnets.
AI.motivation: The mechanisms stabilizing non-collinear magnetism in centrosymmetric crystals—particularly spin-spin interactions mediated by itinerant electrons like RKKY—remain poorly understood. The authors aim to clarify how finite-Q magnetic order couples with electronic modulations observable via scanning tunneling microscopy.
AI.method: Atomically-resolved scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) imaging of electronic textures across five successive magnetic phases of GdRu2Ge2, combined with a simple numerical modeling scheme that maps the underlying spin structures onto predicted electronic density-of-state textures for Ru 4d orbitals on two bond-centered sublattices of the Gd square net.
AI.result: Multi-Q magnetism among Gd 4f spins is shown to entail a corresponding multi-Q texture among Ru 4d orbitals in all five magnetic phases, including two nano-scale skyrmion crystal phases. The alignment between nearest-neighbor Gd spins tightly correlates with the local density-of-states of Ru 4d orbitals on the bond-centered sublattices.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a microscopic view of atomic-scale intertwining of charge and spin degrees-of-freedom in non-collinear itinerant magnets, suggesting that itinerant electron-mediated interactions drive and reflect the complex magnetic order in these materials.

title: Computing Shear Viscosities from Molecular Dynamics Simulation: Comparing the OrthoBoXY Approach with the Green-Kubo Method
summary: We calculated shear viscosities of 15 neat molecular liquids from equilibrium molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the OrthoBoXY approach and compare them to viscosities calculated via the Green-Kubo method. Data from both methods agree very well. Here, we show how to avoid pitfalls while computing the OrthoBoXY-data to obtain optimal results. From simulations of multiple system sizes, we could verify that the viscosity of molecular liquids is not influenced by finite size effects down to systems as small as 250 molecules. Moreover, we demonstrate that also the standard error of the viscosity is nearly independent of the system size. This is shown to be a consequence of a compensation effect of an increasing accuracy of the self-diffusion coefficients with increasing systems-size and the system-size dependent weighting according to the OrthoBoXY-equation. As a consequence, we suggest that it is preferable to run simulations of smaller systems with longer simulation times rather than larger systems with shorter simulation runs. In addition, we discuss a refinement of the recently introduced "recipe" for OrthoBoXY simulations block-lengths $τ_\mathrm{block}$. Based on data from simulations with varying run-lengths, we suggest the following modification: for highly viscous systems, the value of $τ_\mathrm{block}$ might safely be scaled by a factor of $1/8$, significantly reducing the computational resources needed. For less viscous systems, the value of $τ_\mathrm{block}$ might safely be scaled by a factor of $1/4$. For systems with high fluidity, the value of $τ_\mathrm{block}$ should not be scaled down in order to achieve reliable results. When using a smaller system size of 250 molecules, these refinements are leading up to a 24-fold reduction in computational cost compared to the previous recommended set-up without sacrificing numerical accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks OrthoBoXY shear viscosity calculations against the Green-Kubo method for 15 neat molecular liquids using equilibrium MD simulations, showing excellent agreement. It demonstrates that viscosity is free of finite-size effects down to 250 molecules, and that statistical error is nearly system-size independent due to a compensation effect. The authors refine the OrthoBoXY block-length recipe, proposing scaling factors of 1/8 for highly viscous, 1/4 for moderately viscous, and no scaling for highly fluid systems, achieving up to 24-fold computational cost reduction with smaller systems.
AI.motivation: To validate and optimize the OrthoBoXY method for computing shear viscosities of molecular liquids from equilibrium MD simulations, including understanding finite-size effects, statistical error behavior, and reducing computational cost through refined simulation protocols.
AI.method: Equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations of 15 neat molecular liquids; shear viscosities computed via both OrthoBoXY and Green-Kubo methods for cross-validation; multiple system sizes (down to 250 molecules) tested for finite-size effects; varying simulation run-lengths used to refine the OrthoBoXY block-length (τ_block) recommendation.
AI.result: OrthoBoXY and Green-Kubo viscosities agree very well. No finite-size effects on viscosity down to 250 molecules, and standard error is nearly size-independent due to compensation between improved self-diffusion accuracy and OrthoBoXY weighting. The refined recipe allows τ_block to be scaled by 1/8 for highly viscous, 1/4 for less viscous systems, and not at all for highly fluid systems, yielding up to 24-fold computational savings.
AI.conclusion: Smaller systems with longer simulation times are preferable over larger systems with shorter runs for OrthoBoXY viscosity calculations. The refined block-length scaling rules enable significant computational cost reductions (up to 24-fold) without sacrificing numerical accuracy.

title: An Effective String Theory Toolbox for Quantum Hall Interfaces III: Open Worldsheets, Endpoint Conditions, and Branes
summary: A freely moving quantum Hall (QH) interface may end on a physical edge or topological boundary, but fixed-edge theory cannot determine what endpoint data make such a termination consistent. Here we formulate an open-worldsheet junction framework in which the embedding, material charge, anomaly flow, and topological boundary condition are organized together. The endpoint is specified by a geometric support and variational boundary data, together with condensable topological sectors and any outgoing channels required to absorb or continue the worldsheet flux. This construction extends the charge--shape relation to an interval and shows why a lone chiral Majorana cannot terminate on a finite-dimensional endpoint degree of freedom. It gives an operational definition of a QH brane and a systematic basis for endpoint and network theories of dynamical QH interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates an open-worldsheet junction framework to describe how a quantum Hall interface terminates on physical or topological boundaries, organizing the embedding geometry, material charge, anomaly flow, and topological boundary conditions into a unified framework.
AI.motivation: Fixed-edge theory cannot determine what endpoint data make a freely moving quantum Hall interface consistent when it terminates on a physical edge or topological boundary.
AI.method: The authors introduce an open-worldsheet junction framework that organizes the embedding, material charge, anomaly flow, and topological boundary condition together. The endpoint is specified by a geometric support and variational boundary data, along with condensable topological sectors and outgoing channels needed to absorb or continue worldsheet flux.
AI.result: The framework extends the charge-shape relation to an interval, explains why a lone chiral Majorana cannot terminate on a finite-dimensional endpoint degree of freedom, provides an operational definition of a quantum Hall brane, and establishes a systematic basis for endpoint and network theories of dynamical quantum Hall interfaces.
AI.conclusion: The open-worldsheet junction framework provides a complete and systematic description of how dynamical quantum Hall interfaces terminate, including the consistency conditions required at endpoints and the extension to network theories.

title: Landscape of incompressible crystals of hard-core bosons on the square-kagome lattice
summary: We investigate a hard-core boson model on the square-kagome lattice using hierarchical mean-field theory beyond the conventional unit-cell description. We show that the conventional description of the square-kagome lattice based on its smallest unit cell does not fully capture the hierarchy of incompressible states supported by the lattice, but only captures the two compact-localized-state-based phases at densities $5/6$ and $2/3$. Within our approach, we reproduce these previously established phases and uncover additional incompressible states enabled by enlarging the variational cluster. Among these, the $ρ=3/4$ phase is found to be particularly robust, which, through the Matsubara-Matsuda mapping, corresponds to a half-magnetization plateau in the spin-$1/2$ XXZ model. We further apply our approach to two experimentally relevant square-kagome compounds using exchange parameters obtained from first-principles calculations. The calculated magnetization processes are in good agreement with available experimental results and predict additional plateau structures in these materials.

It reproduces known incompressible phases at densities 5/6 and 2/3 while uncovering additional ones (notably a robust ρ=3/4 phase corresponding to a half-magnetization plateau in the spin-1/2 XXZ model via Matsubara-Matsuda mapping). The approach is applied to two experimental square-kagome compounds, yielding magnetization processes in good agreement with experiments and predicting additional plateau structures.
AI.motivation: The conventional smallest-unit-cell description of the square-kagome lattice fails to capture the full hierarchy of incompressible states supported by the lattice. The authors aim to go beyond this limitation to fully characterize the phase diagram and connect theoretical predictions to experimental observables in real materials.
AI.method: Hierarchical mean-field theory with an enlarged variational cluster on the square-kagome lattice, applied to a hard-core boson model; the Matsubara-Matsuda mapping is used to connect boson densities to spin magnetizations in the spin-1/2 XXZ model; exchange parameters from first-principles calculations are used for experimental compounds.
AI.result: The enlarged variational cluster reproduces the previously known 5/6 and 2/3 density phases and uncovers additional incompressible states, with the ρ=3/4 phase being particularly robust and corresponding to a half-magnetization plateau. Application to two square-kagome compounds yields magnetization processes in good agreement with experiment and predicts new plateau structures.
AI.conclusion: The conventional unit-cell description is insufficient for the square-kagome lattice; an enlarged-cluster hierarchical mean-field approach reveals a richer set of incompressible states, including a robust half-magnetization plateau, with direct relevance to real square-kagome compounds as confirmed by experimental agreement and new predictions.

title: Emergent Surface Altermagnetism
summary: Research on altermagnetism has thus far primarily focused on spin-polarized bulk electronic states in magnetic materials. In this work, we advance the field by introducing the concept of surface altermagnetism (SAM), wherein altermagnetic spin polarization emerges at the surfaces of collinear antiferromagnets (AFMs) or altermagnets (AMs). To lay the theoretical groundwork for this phenomenon, we construct a thorough symmetry-based framework that systematically connects bulk spin groups to surface spin groups for both types of systems. Through symmetry analysis, we identify all symmetry-breaking surfaces capable of supporting SAM, identifying 35 for $PT$-symmetric AFMs and 61 distinct cases for bulk AMs. Moreover, we show that 203 collinear spin space groups---including 100 without and 103 with the $[C_2 \Vert P]$ operation---permit the appearance of SAM on the surface of $tT$-symmetric AFMs via the breaking of fractional translational symmetries. The proposed framework is verified using tight-binding models and first-principles calculations, with practical material implementations shown in representative compounds like NaMnP, LiMnAs, and CrSb. Our results establish SAM as a robust, symmetry-protected magnetic state, extending altermagnetic phenomena to material surfaces and paving the way for advanced, field-free spin manipulation in next-generation spintronic technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of surface altermagnetism (SAM), where altermagnetic spin polarization emerges at the surfaces of collinear antiferromagnets or altermagnets. The authors develop a symmetry-based framework connecting bulk and surface spin groups, identify specific symmetry-breaking surfaces capable of supporting SAM (35 for PT-symmetric AFMs, 61 for bulk AMs, and 203 collinear spin space groups for SAM appearance), and verify their framework with tight-binding models and first-principles calculations on materials like NaMnP, LiMnAs, and CrSb.
AI.motivation: Previous research on altermagnetism has focused primarily on bulk electronic states in magnetic materials. This work aims to extend altermagnetic phenomena to material surfaces by introducing the concept of surface altermagnetism, enabling field-free spin manipulation for next-generation spintronic applications.
AI.method: The authors construct a systematic symmetry-based framework (spin group theory) that connects bulk spin groups to surface spin groups for both collinear antiferromagnets and altermagnets. They perform symmetry analysis to enumerate all symmetry-breaking surfaces supporting SAM (35 for PT-symmetric AFMs, 61 for bulk AMs, and 203 collinear spin space groups including 100 without and 103 with [C2 || P] operations). The framework is verified using tight-binding models and first-principles calculations, with material implementations in NaMnP, LiMnAs, and CrSb.
AI.result: The authors identify all symmetry-breaking surfaces supporting SAM: 35 cases for PT-symmetric antiferromagnets and 61 distinct cases for bulk altermagnets. They show that 203 collinear spin space groups permit SAM on tT-symmetric AFM surfaces via breaking of fractional translational symmetries. The framework is validated with tight-binding models and first-principles calculations in representative compounds including NaMnP, LiMnAs, and CrSb.
AI.conclusion: Surface altermagnetism is established as a robust, symmetry-protected magnetic state that extends altermagnetic phenomena to material surfaces. This discovery paves the way for advanced, field-free spin manipulation in next-generation spintronic technologies.

title: Dynamic scaling behavior in the presence of a periodic magnetic driving across Ising continuous transitions
summary: We study the critical dynamics arising from a time-dependent periodic homogenous source coupled to the order-parameter field, which drives a classical ferromagnetic system across a continuous transition. For this purpose, we consider the paradigmatic two-dimensional (2D) Ising model in the presence of a periodic magnetic field $h(t)=-A\, \cos (2πt/P)$, evolving under a purely relaxational dynamics at the critical temperature. We show that the periodic driving gives rise to a peculiar dynamic scaling behavior in the thermodynamic limit, arising from a nontrivial interplay among the time $t$, the amplitude $A$ and period $P$ of $h(t)$. The relevant scaling variables are $τ=t/P$ and $σ=A P^κ$, with $κ= y_h/z$, where $y_h=(d+2-η)/2$ is the critical dimension of the magnetic field, and $z$ is dynamic exponent for the critical relaxational dynamics ($κ\approx 0.865$ for the 2D Ising model). The dynamic scaling behaviors of the magnetization and bond-energy density show an oscillatory behavior around a smooth curve which approaches a large-$τ$ stationary behavior. We also briefly discuss the dynamic behavior of an Ising system driven across the critical point by a periodic time-varying temperature at zero magnetic field.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the critical dynamics of the 2D Ising model driven by a periodically oscillating magnetic field at critical temperature, revealing novel dynamic scaling behavior governed by scaling variables τ=t/P and σ=AP^κ (where κ=y_h/z ≈ 0.865), with magnetization and bond-energy density exhibiting oscillatory behavior around a smooth curve that approaches a stationary large-τ limit.
AI.motivation: To understand how time-dependent periodic driving forces affect critical dynamics in classical ferromagnetic systems, specifically investigating the nontrivial interplay between time, amplitude, and period of the driving field at the critical point.
AI.method: The authors study the 2D Ising model with a periodic magnetic field h(t)=-A cos(2πt/P) under purely relaxational dynamics at the critical temperature, analyzing dynamic scaling behavior in the thermodynamic limit through the scaling variables τ=t/P and σ=AP^κ, where κ=y_h/z with y_h=(d+2-η)/2 and z the dynamic exponent.
AI.result: The periodic driving produces a peculiar dynamic scaling behavior arising from the nontrivial interplay among time t, amplitude A, and period P. The magnetization and bond-energy density show oscillatory behavior around a smooth curve that converges to a large-τ stationary state. The relevant scaling variable is σ=AP^κ with κ≈0.865 for the 2D Ising model. The paper also briefly discusses the case of periodic time-varying temperature driving at zero magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: Periodic driving near a continuous transition leads to a novel dynamic scaling scenario characterized by the scaling variable σ=AP^κ, demonstrating that the interplay between driving amplitude and period fundamentally shapes the nonequilibrium critical dynamics of the Ising system.

title: Dissipation-induced bulk and boundary criticality in the Haldane chain
summary: We study the Haldane chain coupled to a dissipative ohmic bath. Using large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we identify a second-order quantum phase transition into an antiferromagnetic state with spontaneously broken SO(3) symmetry that is governed by an interacting fixed point with dynamical exponent $z\approx 2$. We derive a generalized string order parameter which indicates that the symmetry-protected topological ground state of the Haldane chain is stable for weak dissipation and develops a nontrivial scaling dimension at criticality. In particular, its topological edge modes display nontrivial boundary criticality that is distinct from an equivalent transition out of a trivial state; for the latter, we perform an accurate $ε$ expansion of a dissipative $φ^4$ theory with ordinary boundary conditions. Our setup realizes a spin impurity in a critical yet nonconformal antiferromagnet and paves the way for continuously tunable boundary criticality controlled by dissipation.

The authors derive a generalized string order parameter showing the symmetry-protected topological ground state remains stable under weak dissipation and acquires a nontrivial scaling dimension at criticality. The topological edge modes exhibit boundary criticality distinct from a trivial-state transition, which they analyze via ε-expansion of a dissipative φ⁴ theory with ordinary boundary conditions. This realizes a spin impurity in a critical, nonconformal antiferromagnet and enables continuously tunable boundary criticality via dissipation.
AI.motivation: To understand how symmetry-protected topological (SPT) states behave under strong coupling to a dissipative environment, and to investigate whether the topological edge modes and boundary criticality can be controlled or tuned by dissipation—an open question bridging condensed matter topology and open quantum systems.
AI.method: Large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a Haldane chain coupled to an ohmic dissipative bath, combined with analytical ε-expansion of a dissipative φ⁴ theory with ordinary boundary conditions for the trivial-state transition comparison. A generalized string order parameter is derived to probe the SPT order under dissipation.
AI.result: A second-order quantum phase transition into an antiferromagnetic state with spontaneously broken SO(3) symmetry occurs at an interacting fixed point with dynamical exponent z≈2. The SPT ground state is stable under weak dissipation, and the topological edge modes show boundary criticality distinct from the trivial-state transition.
AI.conclusion: The system realizes a spin impurity in a critical, nonconformal antiferromagnet, and the dissipation-controlled boundary criticality provides a continuously tunable framework for studying topological boundaries in open quantum systems.

title: Interface Engineering of Helium Confinement in Argon-Preplated MCM-41 Nanopores
summary: Atomic-scale modification of mesopore interfaces provides a route to tune the confinement experienced by adsorbed fluids, but how a specific interface preparation translates into the resulting microscopic confinement potential remains unclear. Here, we show that preplating MCM-41 with an argon monolayer modifies the effective pore interface by occupying strongly attractive regions of the heterogeneous silica surface and screening its atomic-scale corrugation. Grand-canonical Monte Carlo simulations of argon adsorption, low-temperature molecular dynamics, and helium test-particle insertion are combined with adsorption isotherms and neutron-scattering measurements to characterize the preplated pore at the atomic scale. Helium test-particle insertion calculations show that the modified interface shifts the helium adsorption minimum to an annular region inside the pore and produces a confinement landscape dominated by a smooth radial component. The resulting radial confinement potential can be described by a continuum cylindrical model, providing microscopic support for the effective potential used in earlier quantum Monte Carlo studies. Residual corrugation persists over multiple spatial scales and is accurately captured by a Gaussian process surrogate. These results demonstrate how atomic preplating can tailor nanopore confinement and provide an experimentally constrained microscopic potential for predictive studies of confined quantum fluids.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that preplating MCM-41 with an argon monolayer modifies the effective pore interface by occupying strongly attractive silica surface regions and screening atomic-scale corrugation, shifting the confinement landscape to a smooth radial component describable by a continuum cylindrical model. The result is an experimentally constrained microscopic potential for predictive studies of confined quantum fluids.
AI.motivation: Atomic-scale modification of mesopore interfaces can tune confinement experienced by adsorbed fluids, but it remains unclear how a specific interface preparation translates into the resulting microscopic confinement potential.
AI.method: The authors combine grand-canonical Monte Carlo simulations of argon adsorption, low-temperature molecular dynamics, and helium test-particle insertion with experimental adsorption isotherms and neutron-scattering measurements to characterize the argon-preplated MCM-41 pore at the atomic scale.
AI.result: Helium test-particle insertion shows the modified interface shifts the helium adsorption minimum to an annular region inside the pore, producing a confinement landscape dominated by a smooth radial component. The radial confinement potential is describable by a continuum cylindrical model, matching the effective potential used in earlier quantum Monte Carlo studies. Residual corrugation spans multiple spatial scales and is accurately captured by a Gaussian process surrogate.
AI.conclusion: Atomic preplating can tailor nanopore confinement, and the resulting experimentally constrained microscopic potential enables predictive studies of confined quantum fluids.

title: Unconventional Scaling of Electric Hall Effect in Magnetic Weyl Semimetals
summary: Electric Hall Effect (EHE), a unique phenomenon in two-dimensional (2D) magnetic systems, refers to the generation of Hall current by an out-of-plane electric field $\Ez$. Here, we demonstrate that for 2D magnetic Weyl semimetals that host doubly degenerate nodal points, the EHE features multiple unconventional scaling laws. At zero temperature, the EHE exhibits a topological $E_F^{-1}$ Fermi-energy scaling. Remarkably, the prefactor of the scaling is determined by the global topological charge of the point without any dependence on the local parameters of the system, leading to a universal and significant enhancement of Hall response in any species of Weyl points as the Fermi energy approaches the Weyl point. This significant response enables a weak electric field to be directly converted into a measurable Hall signal. Surprisingly, this enhanced Hall response is not diminished by temperature, but evolves into an unconventional logarithmically corrected scaling at finite temperature $σ_{xy}\propto\Ez\ln(1/|\Ez|)$ for weak $\Ez$, still yielding a divergent electric-field susceptibility. Thus, our work not only unveils intriguing scaling laws resulting from the interaction between magnetism and topology, but also suggests a novel scaling-enhanced and temperature-robust mechanism that may enable weak electric-field sensing through a practical and all-electric route.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the Electric Hall Effect (EHE) in 2D magnetic Weyl semimetals exhibits multiple unconventional scaling laws: a topological E_F^{-1} Fermi-energy scaling at zero temperature with a universal prefactor determined by the global topological charge, and a logarithmically corrected scaling σ_xy ∝ E_z ln(1/|E_z|) at finite temperature for weak electric fields, yielding a divergent electric-field susceptibility. This suggests a scaling-enhanced, temperature-robust mechanism for all-electric weak-field sensing.
AI.motivation: To explore the Electric Hall Effect (EHE)—generation of Hall current by an out-of-plane electric field—in 2D magnetic Weyl semimetals, and to understand the scaling laws that arise from the interplay between magnetism and topology, potentially enabling practical all-electric sensing of weak electric fields.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of 2D magnetic Weyl semimetals hosting doubly degenerate nodal points, deriving the EHE response at both zero and finite temperature. The zero-temperature analysis reveals a topological E_F^{-1} scaling whose prefactor is set solely by the global topological charge of the Weyl point. Finite-temperature analysis examines the behavior for weak out-of-plane electric fields E_z.
AI.result: At zero temperature, the EHE scales as E_F^{-1} with a universal prefactor independent of local system parameters, determined only by the global topological charge, giving a significant Hall enhancement as Fermi energy approaches the Weyl point. At finite temperature, the Hall response evolves to σ_xy ∝ E_z ln(1/|E_z|) for weak E_z, which paradoxically is not suppressed by temperature and still yields a divergent electric-field susceptibility.
AI.conclusion: The work unveils intriguing unconventional scaling laws from the interaction between magnetism and topology in 2D Weyl semimetals, and proposes a novel scaling-enhanced, temperature-robust mechanism enabling weak electric-field sensing through a practical all-electric route.

title: Resilient strange metal at an unconventional quantum critical point in $d=2$
summary: Properties of the two-dimensional Hubbard model with nearest-neighbor hopping are under scrutiny in cold-atom experiments and diagrammatic quantum Monte Carlo. Given the controlled nature of these approaches, it is timely to make predictions about strange-metal behavior and its relation to quantum-critical properties. Even for interaction strengths below the Mott transition, several peculiarities occur at the quantum critical point separating Fermi liquid and incommensurate spin-density wave order. Here, we predict, using the non-perturbative improved two-particle self-consistent approach, that for correlation lengths ranging from about one to one hundred lattice spacings, Kohn anomalies on the underlying Fermi surface lead to unconventional critical exponents. The temperature dependence of the single-particle self-energy acquires strong momentum dependence along the Fermi surface with no clear evidence of Landau quasiparticles. Nevertheless, we observe strange-metal behavior, namely, resistivity that scales linearly with temperature as $T\rightarrow{0}$. Our work shows that a linear temperature dependence of resistivity arises without a linear-in-temperature self-energy along the Fermi surface, as is often assumed.

AI.tldr: Using the improved two-particle self-consistent (TPSC) approach, the authors predict that near the quantum critical point separating Fermi liquid and incommensurate spin-density wave order in the 2D Hubbard model, Kohn anomalies on the Fermi surface lead to unconventional critical exponents. For correlation lengths of 1-100 lattice spacings, the self-energy acquires strong momentum dependence with no clear Landau quasiparticles, yet resistivity scales linearly with temperature as T→0—demonstrating that linear-in-T resistivity can arise without a linear-in-T self-energy along the Fermi surface.
AI.motivation: To make controlled, non-perturbative predictions about strange-metal behavior and its relation to quantum-critical properties in the two-dimensional Hubbard model, which is now directly addressable via cold-atom experiments and diagrammatic quantum Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.method: The authors employ the non-perturbative improved two-particle self-consistent (TPSC) approach to compute single-particle self-energies and transport properties near the quantum critical point separating Fermi liquid and incommensurate spin-density wave order, for interaction strengths below the Mott transition.
AI.result: For correlation lengths from ~1 to ~100 lattice spacings, Kohn anomalies on the Fermi surface generate unconventional critical exponents. The self-energy's temperature dependence acquires strong momentum dependence along the Fermi surface without clear Landau quasiparticles, yet resistivity exhibits linear-in-temperature scaling as T→0, i.e., strange-metal behavior.
AI.conclusion: Linear-in-temperature resistivity can emerge without a linear-in-temperature self-energy along the Fermi surface, challenging the common assumption that strange-metal transport requires such a self-energy. This provides concrete predictions for cold-atom and quantum Monte Carlo studies of quantum-critical strange-metal behavior in the 2D Hubbard model.

title: Magnetic susceptibility of diluted magnetic semiconductors at low carrier densities
summary: We calculate the static longitudinal and the transverse dynamic magnetic susceptibilities of (III,Mn)V diluted magnetic semiconductors, using the random phase approximation, for a simple impurity band model appropriate for the low charge carrier concentration regime. The magnetic susceptibilities are shown to depend sensitively on the amount of positional disorder of the Mn impurities. The results we obtain are consistent with previous studies of the spin wave spectrum and of the spatially inhomogeneous ferromagnetic state of these materials.

AI.tldr: This paper calculates static longitudinal and transverse dynamic magnetic susceptibilities of (III,Mn)V diluted magnetic semiconductors using the random phase approximation within a simple impurity band model valid for low carrier concentrations, finding that the susceptibilities depend sensitively on positional disorder of Mn impurities, consistent with prior work on spin wave spectra and inhomogeneous ferromagnetism.
AI.motivation: To understand how positional disorder of Mn impurities affects the magnetic response (static longitudinal and transverse dynamic susceptibilities) of (III,Mn)V diluted magnetic semiconductors, particularly in the low charge carrier concentration regime.
AI.method: The authors employ the random phase approximation (RPA) within a simple impurity band model appropriate for the low carrier concentration regime to compute both the static longitudinal and transverse dynamic magnetic susceptibilities.
AI.result: The magnetic susceptibilities are shown to depend sensitively on the amount of positional disorder of the Mn impurities. The results agree with previous studies of the spin wave spectrum and the spatially inhomogeneous ferromagnetic state.
AI.conclusion: Positional disorder of Mn impurities plays a crucial role in determining the magnetic susceptibility properties of (III,Mn)V diluted magnetic semiconductors, and the present calculations corroborate earlier findings on spin waves and inhomogeneous ferromagnetism in these materials.

title: Thermodynamic statistics of given names in USA and France
comment: 11 pages, 17 figures, links to arXiv:2512.06420, arXiv:2506.17720, arXiv:2606.17965, arXiv:2607.07315, arXiv:2607.15119
summary: Using official government data sets of USA and France we analyze the occurrence/frequency/popularity distributions of given names on a time scale of more than 100 years. These distributions are characterized through the Lorenz and Pareto curves broadly used in the analysis of wealth inequality in the world. These curves remain stable during the considered time period with the Gini coefficient remaining in the narrow range 0.85-0.95. As for the case of wealth inequality, we show that the distributions of names are well described by the Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation phenomenon well studied in various physical systems. The RJ thermalization results from two integrals of motion being analogous to energy and probability norm conservation in physical systems with energy states corresponding to popularity levels of names. Time correlations between names are also determined showing their stability until the middle of the twentieth century and a significant change after that.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes name frequency distributions in USA and France over 100+ years using Lorenz and Pareto curves from economics. The distributions show remarkable stability (Gini coefficient 0.85-0.95) and are well described by Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation, analogous to physical systems with conserved energy and probability. Time correlations between names were stable until mid-20th century then changed significantly.
AI.motivation: To characterize the statistical distributions of given names over long time scales using tools from wealth inequality analysis, and to determine whether these distributions follow universal physical laws such as Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization.
AI.method: Analysis of official government name datasets from USA and France spanning over 100 years. Distribution characterization using Lorenz curves, Pareto curves, and Gini coefficients. Application of Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization formalism treating popularity levels as energy states, with energy and probability norm as conserved integrals of motion. Computation of time correlations between names.
AI.result: Name distributions remain stable over the entire period with Gini coefficients in the narrow range 0.85-0.95. The distributions are well described by Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation. Time correlations between names remain stable until the middle of the 20th century but undergo significant changes afterward.
AI.conclusion: The statistical physics framework of Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization, originally developed for wealth inequality, successfully models name popularity distributions. This suggests universal statistical laws governing cultural/social phenomena analogous to physical systems, though recent cultural shifts have altered the temporal correlation structure.

title: Geometric closure of classical nucleation theory for magnetic-field-controlled nanoparticle size across magnetic classes
summary: Controlling nanoparticle size during synthesis remains a central challenge in nanoscience, particularly in systems where external magnetic fields are used as continuous control parameters. Existing descriptions of magnetic-field-assisted nucleation are typically material-specific or rely on computationally intensive atomistic methods. Here, we reformulate classical nucleation theory as a geometrically closed thermodynamic framework by introducing a sphere-packing representation of atomic assembly. This construction establishes a direct link between discrete atomic structure and continuum free-energy contributions under applied magnetic fields, yielding a field-driven evolution equation for the critical nucleus size. The resulting theory provides a unified description of nanoparticle nucleation across superparamagnetic, paramagnetic, and diamagnetic systems within a single formalism. It quantitatively reproduces previously unresolved experimental observations for magnetite and nickel nanoparticles, namely the systematic reduction of mean particle size and narrowing of size distributions with increasing magnetic field. In the diamagnetic limit, the framework recovers our earlier analytical susceptibility-based description of silver nanoparticles, in which the field-dependent critical radius is governed by the induced-magnetization contribution to the nucleation free energy. Beyond modeling the reduction of mean particle size with increasing magnetic field, the framework reveals that the narrowing of size distributions emerges naturally from the curvature of the field-modified free-energy landscape. These results establish magnetic-field-assisted nucleation as a geometrically constrained thermodynamic process, providing a computationally efficient route for controlling nanoparticle size across distinct magnetic material classes.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates classical nucleation theory using a sphere-packing representation of atomic assembly, creating a unified geometric thermodynamic framework that describes magnetic-field-assisted nanoparticle nucleation across superparamagnetic, paramagnetic, and diamagnetic systems, quantitatively reproducing experimental observations of size reduction and distribution narrowing in magnetite, nickel, and silver nanoparticles.
AI.motivation: Controlling nanoparticle size during synthesis remains a central challenge in nanoscience, especially in systems using external magnetic fields as continuous control parameters. Existing descriptions of magnetic-field-assisted nucleation are either material-specific or computationally intensive (atomistic methods), lacking a unified, efficient theoretical framework.
AI.method: The paper reformulates classical nucleation theory as a geometrically closed thermodynamic framework by introducing a sphere-packing representation of atomic assembly. This connects discrete atomic structure to continuum free-energy contributions under applied magnetic fields, producing a field-driven evolution equation for the critical nucleus size within a single formalism covering superparamagnetic, paramagnetic, and diamagnetic systems.
AI.result: The framework quantitatively reproduces experimental observations for magnetite and nickel nanoparticles, including systematic reduction of mean particle size and narrowing of size distributions with increasing magnetic field. It also recovers the earlier analytical susceptibility-based description for diamagnetic silver nanoparticles. The framework reveals that distribution narrowing emerges naturally from the curvature of the field-modified free-energy landscape.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic-field-assisted nucleation is established as a geometrically constrained thermodynamic process, providing a computationally efficient route for controlling nanoparticle size across distinct magnetic material classes.

title: Anatomy of Spin--Orbit Torques in Monolayer Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ and Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$: Insights from atomistic and momentum-space decompositions
summary: We present a systematic first-principles study of the spin-orbit torques in the ferromagnetic monolayers Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ (FGT) and Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ (FGaT). Despite sharing the same crystal structure (point group $D_{3h}$) and predominantly Fe~$3d$ spin-polarized bands, the two materials exhibit markedly different current-induced torques. We reveal these differences by computing the full angular dependence of the torkance---the torque per unit applied electric field---using linear-response theory with symmetry-adapted spin--orbit-coupled Wannier functions. FGaT may be viewed as a hole-doped analogue of FGT, since Ga contributes one valence electron fewer than Ge. Although the work functions differ by only about $28$~meV, the band filling near $K$ and $K'$ changes substantially: the density of states at $\varepsilon_F$ is reduced by a factor of three and its spin polarization reverses from majority in FGT to minority in FGaT. These electronic changes are reflected in the torques resolved by time-reversal parity, sublattice, and momentum. In particular, we identify pronounced hidden torques in FGaT and relate the suppression of its fourth-harmonic Fermi-sea component to the evolution of momentum-space pockets. Finally, we discuss the emergence of such self-torques, which are not captured by the conventional picture of current-induced spin accumulation, within a symmetry-based phenomenological framework. Our results provide microscopic insight into current-induced torques in two-dimensional ferromagnets and offer guidance for defect and van der Waals engineering of layered magnetic materials.

AI.tldr: A first-principles study comparing spin-orbit torques in ferromagnetic monolayers Fe₃GeTe₂ and Fe₃GaTe₂, revealing markedly different torque behaviors despite identical crystal structures, and explaining these differences through band-filling, spin-polarization, and momentum-space changes.
AI.motivation: To understand why two ferromagnetic monolayers with the same crystal structure (point group D₃h) and similar Fe 3d spin-polarized bands exhibit markedly different current-induced torques, providing microscopic insight into torques in 2D ferromagnets and guidance for material engineering.
AI.method: First-principles linear-response theory using symmetry-adapted spin-orbit-coupled Wannier functions to compute the full angular dependence of the torkance (torque per unit electric field), with torques resolved by time-reversal parity, sublattice, and momentum.
AI.result: FGaT acts as a hole-doped analogue of FGT (Ga has one fewer valence electron than Ge). Although work functions differ by only 28 meV, band filling near K/K' changes substantially: density of states at εF is reduced by a factor of three and spin polarization reverses from majority (FGT) to minority (FGaT). Pronounced hidden torques are identified in FGaT, and suppression of its fourth-harmonic Fermi-sea component is linked to momentum-space pocket evolution.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals that subtle valence-electron differences between structurally identical materials strongly alter spin-orbit torques, discusses emergence of self-torques beyond conventional spin-accumulation pictures within a symmetry-based phenomenological framework, and offers guidance for defect and van der Waals engineering of layered magnetic materials.

title: Collective search-and-capture under competing assignment policies
summary: We study a minimal lattice model of active search-and-capture in which persistent random walkers locate and irreversibly capture immobile targets through a finite-range, mutually exclusive assignment rule. We measure the collective completion time $T_c$ as a function of the walkers' reorientation rate $α$ and the search radius $R$. The dependence $T_c(α)$ is non-monotonic, with a minimum at intermediate persistence whose depth decreases as $R$ grows. Capture kinetics show that $T_c$ is not a typical capture time but is governed by the extreme, late-time tail of the capture process, while the bulk of targets are captured much earlier; this tail is controlled mainly by the free-exploration phase rather than by the final directed approach. We then compare the baseline single-round assignment rule with cascading reassignment and with maximum-cardinality matching on a candidate graph. The two greedy policies (single-round and cascading) agree at very small $R$, whereas maximum-cardinality matching already produces a strong speedup at moderate $R$: improved matching reduces $T_c$ by factors of several at large $R$, and by more than an order of magnitude at moderate $R$. Thus, in this collective, depletion-coupled search problem, the assignment policy can control the capture time more strongly than the walkers' persistence.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a minimal lattice model of active search-and-capture where persistent random walkers irreversibly capture immobile targets via a mutually exclusive assignment rule. The collective completion time Tc is non-monotonic in reorientation rate α, minimized at intermediate persistence, and this minimum weakens as search radius R grows. Tc is governed by the extreme late-time tail of capture rather than typical capture kinetics. Comparing assignment policies, maximum-cardinality matching on a candidate graph dramatically outperforms greedy single-round and cascading policies, especially at moderate R where speedups exceed an order of magnitude.
AI.motivation: To understand how persistence and assignment policy jointly control collective completion time in depletion-coupled active search-and-capture processes, where the search is dominated by extreme late-time events rather than typical capture dynamics.
AI.method: A minimal lattice model with persistent random walkers and immobile targets using a finite-range mutually exclusive assignment rule. Varied walker reorientation rate α and search radius R, measuring collective completion time Tc(α,R). Compared three assignment policies: single-round greedy, cascading reassignment, and maximum-cardinality matching on a candidate graph.
AI.result: Tc(α) is non-monotonic with a minimum at intermediate persistence, whose depth decreases as R grows. Tc reflects extreme tail dynamics controlled mainly by the free-exploration phase, not directed approach. Greedy policies (single-round and cascading) agree only at very small R, while maximum-cardinality matching yields speedups of several-fold at large R and more than an order of magnitude at moderate R.
AI.conclusion: In collective depletion-coupled search problems, the assignment policy can control capture time more strongly than the walkers' persistence, highlighting that optimal matching strategies are crucial for accelerating completion in multi-agent search-and-capture tasks.

title: Anyon-Impurity Bound States in Quantum-Engineered Fractional Chern Insulators
summary: Mobile impurities provide a powerful means of probing correlated and topological quantum matter, through their dressing by the surrounding medium and the practical probes granting access to the resulting composite object. Motivated by the recent observation of anyon-impurity composites in the solid state, as well as recent realizations of Laughlin-type states in engineered lattice systems, we investigate the formation of a bound state between a mobile impurity and a single pinned quasihole in the interacting Harper-Hofstadter model deep in the fractional Chern insulator regime. Combining analytical arguments with large-scale numerical simulations, we characterize the structure, energetics, and stability of hybrid anyon-impurity bound states, and show that their binding energy provides direct access to the fractional charge of the quasihole under conditions that we identify. We further demonstrate that the composite object can be coherently transported by externally steering the quasihole pinning potential. Our results establish a realistic pathway for controlled anyon-impurity manipulation in quantum-engineered platforms, enabling experimentally feasible protocols for braiding.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the formation of hybrid bound states between a mobile impurity and a single pinned quasihole in the interacting Harper-Hofstadter model deep in the fractional Chern insulator regime, showing that binding energy provides direct access to the fractional quasihole charge and that the composite can be coherently transported for braiding protocols.
AI.motivation: Recent observations of anyon-impurity composites in solid-state systems and realizations of Laughlin-type states in engineered lattices motivate the study of how mobile impurities can probe correlated and topological quantum matter by dressing with the surrounding medium.
AI.method: Combining analytical arguments with large-scale numerical simulations, the authors characterize the structure, energetics, and stability of hybrid anyon-impurity bound states in the interacting Harper-Hofstadter model deep in the fractional Chern insulator regime.
AI.result: The binding energy of the anyon-impurity bound state provides direct access to the fractional charge of the quasihole under identified conditions, and the composite object can be coherently transported by externally steering the quasihole pinning potential.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a realistic pathway for controlled anyon-impurity manipulation in quantum-engineered platforms, enabling experimentally feasible protocols for braiding.

title: Phonon spectral functions of low-density polaron metals
summary: We use the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) to compute the phonon spectral function of a one-dimensional spinless Holstein model doped with a low but finite carrier concentration, $x \leq 0.15$, as a function of the electron-phonon coupling $λ$. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first such results in this regime, complementing extensive prior work at the single-polaron level ($x\to 0$). We find that significant phonon spectral weight is transferred both below, all the way down to $ω=0$, and above the bare phonon energy $Ω$, in stark contrast with the Kohn-anomaly phenomenology expected in the Migdal limit, where weight remains centered near $Ω$ with a kink at $q=2k_F$. No signature of this $2k_F$ kink appears in our results. This behavior is captured qualitatively by the Random Phase Approximation (RPA), and semi-quantitatively, at negligible extra computational cost, by a ``dressed RPA'' scheme in which the electron addition propagator is renormalized using the Momentum Average (MA) approximation for the low-density electron-polaron. By contrast, adding the lowest-order vertex correction to this dressed scheme produces unphysical negative spectral weight, signaling that vertex and propagator dressings must be treated consistently once the propagators are dressed nonperturbatively. Our results provide an efficient approximation for the phonon spectral functions of low-density polaron metals, a regime relevant to weakly doped insulators.

AI.tldr: Using DMRG, the authors compute the phonon spectral function of a 1D spinless Holstein model at low but finite doping (x≤0.15) as a function of electron-phonon coupling λ, finding significant phonon spectral weight transfer both below and above the bare phonon energy with no 2kF kink, in contrast to Migdal-limit Kohn-anomaly expectations. A "dressed RPA" scheme (RPA with MA-renormalized propagators) captures the behavior semi-quantitatively at negligible cost, while adding a simple vertex correction produces unphysical negative spectral weight.
AI.motivation: To extend phonon spectral function studies beyond the single-polaron limit (x→0) into the low but finite carrier concentration regime relevant to weakly doped insulators and polaron metals, where no prior results existed.
AI.method: Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) calculations of the phonon spectral function for the 1D spinless Holstein model at low doping (x≤0.15), compared against RPA and a dressed-RPA scheme where the electron addition propagator is renormalized via the Momentum Average (MA) approximation for the low-density electron-polaron.
AI.result: Phonon spectral weight transfers significantly below (down to ω=0) and above the bare phonon energy Ω, with no 2kF kink. This is captured qualitatively by RPA and semi-quantitatively by the dressed-RPA/MA scheme at negligible cost. Adding a lowest-order vertex correction to the dressed scheme yields unphysical negative spectral weight.
AI.conclusion: The dressed RPA with MA-renormalized propagators provides an efficient, accurate approximation for phonon spectral functions in low-density polaron metals, and vertex corrections must be treated consistently with nonperturbative propagator dressing to avoid unphysical results.

title: Tuning the Optoelectronics of Mixed-Semiconductors through the interplay of Quantum confinement and Stoichiometry Engineering
summary: All-inorganic cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) nanocrystals (NCs) have established themselves as an emerging semiconductor for next-generation optoelectronic technologies due to their unique combination of properties, such as near unity photoluminescence quantum yields, narrow color pure emission, and exceptional defect tolerance. Although size-dependent optical signatures of these NCs are well reported, the complexity of mixed ionic-electronic transport remains largely unexplored. In this study, we provide a comprehensive analysis of size-dependent charge transport by decoupling ionic and electronic transport dynamics through carefully designed transient current and space charge limited current measurements. By employing NCs of different sizes ranging from 5.6 nm to 11.3 nm in thin films, we provide a comprehensive understanding of quantum confinement effects and related synthetic chemistry. Contrary to popular beliefs of quantum confinement and band gap broadening, our results demonstrate that the smallest NCs exhibit the most efficient transport characteristics, evidenced by the lowest activation energy (hole activation energy = 78 meV) for hole transport and the highest barrier for vacancy-mediated ion migration (ion activation energy = 370 meV). This work paves a way forward for perovskite-based efficient quantum devices, by demonstrating that moving into a strong quantum confinement regime, a superior charge transport can be facilitated, when supported by carefully tailored stoichiometry.

AI.tldr: This study systematically decouples ionic and electronic transport in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals of varying sizes (5.6–11.3 nm), revealing that the smallest nanocrystals exhibit the most efficient hole transport (activation energy = 78 meV) and the highest resistance to vacancy-mediated ion migration (activation energy = 370 meV), contrary to expectations of quantum confinement degrading transport.
AI.motivation: While size-dependent optical properties of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals are well-documented, the interplay between ionic and electronic transport—crucial for optoelectronic device performance—remains largely unexplored. Understanding how quantum confinement affects charge transport is essential for optimizing next-generation perovskite-based devices.
AI.method: The authors decoupled ionic and electronic transport dynamics in CsPbBr3 nanocrystal thin films using transient current and space charge limited current measurements. Nanocrystals of five different sizes ranging from 5.6 nm to 11.3 nm were synthesized and characterized to probe the effects of quantum confinement and stoichiometry on charge transport.
AI.result: The smallest nanocrystals demonstrated the most efficient transport characteristics, with the lowest hole activation energy (78 meV) and the highest activation barrier for vacancy-mediated ion migration (370 meV), contradicting conventional assumptions that quantum confinement and band gap broadening would hinder charge transport.
AI.conclusion: Strong quantum confinement, when paired with carefully tailored stoichiometry, can facilitate superior charge transport in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals, paving the way for efficient perovskite-based quantum optoelectronic devices.

title: Transport coefficients in hard-sphere fluids: thermodynamic versus kinetic descriptions
summary: A thermodynamic theory for transport coefficients in hard-sphere fluids is developed from a general expression for the Onsager matrix. The theory predicts the ratio $σ/σ_{\rm id}$, where $σ$ is a transport coefficient and $σ_{\rm id}$ denotes its dilute-gas value. This ratio depends exclusively on equilibrium thermodynamic properties and can therefore be computed directly from the equation of state. Compact expressions are obtained for the thermal conductivity, viscosity, and self-diffusion coefficient. These expressions quantitatively reproduce simulation data over almost the entire fluid range and, in the case of self-diffusion, significantly improve upon the predictions of Enskog kinetic theory. The results demonstrate that transport coefficients can be accurately described within a purely thermodynamic framework.

AI.tldr: A thermodynamic theory for transport coefficients in hard-sphere fluids is derived from the Onsager matrix, predicting transport-to-dilute-gas ratios solely from equilibrium thermodynamic properties (i.e., the equation of state). Compact expressions for thermal conductivity, viscosity, and self-diffusion quantitatively match simulation data across nearly the entire fluid range, with self-diffusion significantly outperforming Enskog theory.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that transport coefficients in dense fluids can be accurately predicted from equilibrium thermodynamic data alone, without requiring kinetic-theory-based corrections, thereby establishing a purely thermodynamic description of transport.
AI.method: Starting from a general expression for the Onsager matrix, the authors derive a thermodynamic framework in which the ratio σ/σ_id depends only on equilibrium thermodynamic properties. Compact closed-form expressions are then obtained for thermal conductivity, viscosity, and self-diffusion coefficients, computable directly from the equation of state.
AI.result: The derived expressions quantitatively reproduce simulation data over almost the entire fluid range. For self-diffusion, the predictions significantly improve upon those of Enskog kinetic theory.
AI.conclusion: Transport coefficients of hard-sphere fluids can be accurately described within a purely thermodynamic framework, establishing a direct connection between equilibrium thermodynamics and transport phenomena.

title: Multi-State Geometry of Density Matrices and Rectification Sum Rules
summary: The geometry of quantum states has emerged as a key ingredient in understanding the linear and nonlinear responses of quantum materials. To date, however, the connection between geometry and nonlinear response is best understood for clean, noninteracting systems at zero temperature. In this work, we develop a theory of multi-state geometry for density matrices and use it to derive sum rules for second-order rectification, making no assumptions about the strength of disorder or interactions. We first show that perturbation theory for thermal density matrices gives rise to two dual information-theoretic connections and an almost complex structure. We introduce a complex, quantum generalization of the Amari-Chentsov tensor of classical information theory, the cQAC tensor, which captures the multi-state geometry of the perturbed density matrix. We derive a zero-temperature sum rule for the frequency-integrated DC rectification response of an insulator as a difference between a ground state third cumulant and the complex distortion tensor, a multi-state geometric quantity built from the cQAC tensor. This generalizes known single-particle sum rules for the shift and nonlinear Hall currents to many-body systems and general perturbations. Specializing to the shift current, we resolve the geometric contribution for multiband insulators into particle-like and hole-like terms. We verify the sum rule numerically in a generalized Kane-Mele model, finding that the geometric contribution can dominate the integrated response. Finally, we show that although the splitting of the sum rule into cumulant and geometric contributions does not survive at nonzero temperature, the measured sum rule for insulators differs from its zero-temperature form by corrections exponentially small in the gap, allowing low-temperature rectification measurements to probe the multi-state geometry of insulators.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a multi-state geometry theory for density matrices and derives sum rules for second-order rectification in quantum materials, valid for arbitrary disorder and interactions, generalizing known single-particle geometric sum rules to many-body systems.
AI.motivation: While the geometry of quantum states is key to understanding nonlinear responses of quantum materials, the connection between geometry and nonlinear response is currently best understood only for clean, noninteracting systems at zero temperature. A theory valid beyond these restrictions is needed.
AI.method: Perturbation theory for thermal density matrices is shown to yield dual information-theoretic connections and an almost complex structure. The authors introduce a complex quantum generalization of the Amari-Chentsov tensor (cQAC tensor) capturing multi-state geometry, from which they derive zero-temperature sum rules for frequency-integrated DC rectification as a difference between a ground-state third cumulant and a complex distortion tensor. The shift-current case is resolved into particle-like and hole-like terms and verified numerically in a generalized Kane-Mele model.
AI.result: A general sum rule for second-order rectification is derived, valid with arbitrary disorder and interactions. The geometric contribution can dominate the integrated response, as shown in a generalized Kane-Mele model. Although the cumulant/geometric splitting does not survive at finite temperature, the measured sum rule for insulators differs from its zero-temperature form only by exponentially small corrections in the gap, enabling low-temperature rectification to probe multi-state geometry.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a general framework for multi-state geometry of density matrices that generalizes known single-particle geometric sum rules (shift and nonlinear Hall currents) to many-body systems with arbitrary disorder and interactions, and shows that low-temperature rectification measurements can probe this geometry in insulators.

title: A Universal Control Budget for First-Passage Kinetics
summary: The first-passage time is the natural observable of reaction completion, yet how its mean responds to a rate change has lacked a general constraint. We show that the logarithmic sensitivity of the mean first-passage time of any finite Markov chain to any rate is bounded by one in magnitude, and that these sensitivities sum to -1. Together the two laws form a conserved control budget: speeding completion through some transitions must be paid for by others, and a coordinated change shifts the completion time only as far as the budget allows. Raising an activation barrier or shifting the depth of a well moves many rates at once, yet neither can shift the completion time further than a single rate could. The budget caps kinetic-proofreading discrimination at the checkpoint count, and prices it in sensitivity to substrate concentration.

AI.tldr: This paper proves two general laws for any finite Markov chain: the logarithmic sensitivity of the mean first-passage time (MFPT) to any individual rate is bounded by one in magnitude, and these sensitivities sum to -1. Together these form a "conserved control budget" that constrains how much rate changes can shift reaction completion times.
AI.motivation: Although first-passage time is a natural observable of reaction completion in stochastic processes, there was previously no general constraint on how its mean responds to changes in transition rates. The authors sought to find universal bounds and conservation laws governing this sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical results for finite Markov chains, proving that the logarithmic sensitivity of the mean first-passage time with respect to any single rate parameter is bounded by one in magnitude, and that the sum of all such sensitivities equals -1.
AI.result: The two laws combine to form a conserved control budget: accelerating completion via some transitions must be compensated by slowing via others, and no single rate (or coordinated change of many rates) can shift completion time beyond this budget. This caps kinetic-proofreading discrimination at the checkpoint count and prices discrimination in terms of substrate concentration sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: These universal bounds provide a fundamental constraint on how rate manipulations can influence mean first-passage times, with direct practical consequences for kinetic proofreading and biochemical reaction speed limits.

title: Calculations of the Krypton Phase Diagram and Novel Plasticity
summary: The phase diagram for Kr, as represented by the Tadah! two-body potential is shown to have face-centred cubic (fcc), hexahonal close packed (hcp), and body centred cubic (bcc) regions. It has been assembled by combining several methods: direct liquid--solid coexistence for the melt lines, Gibbs--Helmholtz integration and Clapeyron slopes for the bcc--fcc line, slab coexistence for the liquid--gas line, static zero-temperature relaxations for the crystals, and the quasiharmonic approximation for the low-temperature fcc--hcp windows. The bcc phase contains highly mobile ``greedy snake" defects, which suggests a reinterpretation of the melt-curve data: the anomaly observed may be due to the speckle method detecting the bcc-fcc boundary, not the melt curve. While pair potentials have limitations, comparison with a foundation MACE model shows that a more flexible machine-learned model does not necessarily improve matters if inappropriately trained.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs the complete phase diagram for krypton using the Tadah! two-body potential by combining multiple computational methods, revealing fcc, hcp, and bcc regions. The bcc phase contains mobile "greedy snake" defects, suggesting that a previously observed anomaly in melt-curve data may actually be the bcc-fcc boundary detected by the speckle method. A comparison with a MACE machine-learned model shows that more flexible models don't necessarily improve predictions if trained inappropriately.
AI.motivation: To assemble a complete and accurate phase diagram for krypton using a modern pair potential, reconciling disparate simulation methods, and to investigate the origin of anomalies in experimental melt-curve data.
AI.method: Combines direct liquid-solid coexistence simulations for melt lines, Gibbs-Helmholtz integration and Clapeyron slopes for the bcc-fcc boundary, slab coexistence for the liquid-gas line, static zero-temperature relaxations for crystals, and quasiharmonic approximation for low-temperature fcc-hcp transitions. Also compares against a MACE machine-learned interatomic potential.
AI.result: The phase diagram exhibits fcc, hcp, and bcc regions. The bcc phase displays highly mobile "greedy snake" defects. The previously observed melt-curve anomaly likely corresponds to the bcc-fcc boundary rather than the true melt curve. The MACE model, despite being more flexible, does not outperform the pair potential when inappropriately trained.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive phase diagram for Kr can be obtained via multi-method combination with pair potentials. The reinterpretation of the experimental anomaly as a solid-solid transition rather than melting has implications for understanding Kr's high-pressure behavior, and caution is warranted when applying machine-learned potentials without appropriate training data.

title: Metal-Coordination Effects on the Stability and ORR/OER Activity of Layered Organometallic Single-Atom Catalysts: A Theoretical Study
summary: Organometallic layered materials have emerged as promising single-atom catalysts for oxygen reduction and evolution reactions, but their practical use has been limited by insufficient electrochemical stability. Here, we present a density functional theory study clarifying the relationship between catalytic activity and stability in organometallic single-atom catalysts with metal-N$_4$ (MN$_4$) and metal-O$_4$ (MO$_4$) coordination. We compare graphene-embedded MN$_4$ motif and phthalocyanine-like frameworks with MO$_4$-coordination frameworks, including M$_4$(OHPTP)$_2$ and M$_3$(HHTP)$_2$ (M = Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn). Stability is assessed by surface Pourbaix analysis, while activity is evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode method. MN$_4$ systems show competitive overpotentials but suffer strong pH-dependent instability. In contrast, MO$_4$ frameworks exhibit enhanced robustness across wide pH ranges while maintaining good catalytic performance. A proposed stability descriptor enables direct comparison across systems, identifying MO$_4$ coordination structures, particularly M$_4$(OHPTP)$_2$ (M = Zn, Co) as optimal for balancing activity and stability in practical electrocatalysis.
